items.summary:
The NVIDIA Board of Directors has established a new standing committee to provide board-level oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management. The newly created National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will retain independent outside experts for legal, national security, and trade compliance expertise as it supports its work.

Director Suzanne Nora Johnson has been appointed chair of the committee, with directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri serving as members. NVIDIA's existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to both the Committee and Interim CEO Colette Kress on day-to-day operations. The committee is expected to meet at least quarterly, including in sessions with management and in executive session.

The committee will oversee efforts to strengthen the internal National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team while working closely with independent third-party experts in law, national security, and global trade compliance. In a statement, Harvey Jones, Chairman of NVIDIA's Board of Directors, said that "NVIDIA recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security." He added that as "the world's leading advanced computing company," NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead in addressing these challenges while safeguarding national security and supporting continued technological innovation.

The decision reflects the Board's further commitment to enhance its engagement with relevant government stakeholders and demonstrate high standards of governance and oversight.
items.title: NVIDIA Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee

AI chip giant Nvidia is set to report its first earnings since November 12, when co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The revelations intensified scrutiny of a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere using US hardware not available for export to China. In response, Washington announced new restrictions on November 16 requiring licences for advanced chip exports to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil — countries the US commerce department says present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The scandal has battered Nvidia's shares, which until recently made it the world's most valuable publicly traded company at the centre of an AI build-out that helped propel markets to record highs.

The new export curbs and wider fallout from Huang's affair risk casting a shadow over talks between US President Donald Trump and Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which begins on November 18 in Shenzhen. Beijing condemned the measures through foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun, who said China would take necessary steps to safeguard its rights and interests.

Nvidia's third quarter results are scheduled for release at 6 am Singapore time (10 pm GMT) on November 17 — though one source frames this as the first earnings since the scandal. The report will be presented under interim CEO Colette Kress, who is serving after Huang's departure. Investors will scrutinise whether Kress will slow his aggressive investment strategy and watch for guidance on future sales and chip demand in Asia, particularly Singapore.

The situation has exposed a rift within the Trump administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accusing the commerce department of ignoring reports that Megaspeed — a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation since 2024 — was helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia chips. Alice Huang, the affair partner (unrelated to Jensen), is a former executive of Megaspeed.

Analysts warn that a business-as-usual tone in the earnings call would likely be poorly received; Jacob Bourne of Emarketer cautioned against such an approach. The results could ripple across AI investments propping up the US economy, including Nvidia's backing of major labs like Anthropic, whose Claude chatbot is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on November 19. Meanwhile, tech firms dragged Asian stock markets down again on November 17 as uncertainty mounted.

On a regional level, Singapore said it was engaging with affected companies and exploring how to facilitate trusted access to AI chips for its own firms, while Indonesia reviewed the measure and sought industry input on potential impacts on operations and investment in the data centre sector.
items.title: Nvidia's First Post-Scandal Earnings Amid US Export Curbs and Geopolitical Tensions

items.summary:
George Soros’ family office joined a group of at least a dozen ultra-wealthy investment firms in trimming their Nvidia holdings during the quarter ended September 30, according to Bloomberg data compiled from quarterly regulatory filings. The billionaire’s namesake money manager cut its stake by almost a fifth — the largest disclosed reduction for its Nvidia holding in 2026 after it had previously added to the position. Michael Platt’s BlueCrest Capital Management and an investment firm serving Abu Dhabi ruler Sheikh Mohamed Bin Zayed Al Nahyan also reduced their stakes over the same period, though all selling family offices retained at least some shares, with combined holdings exceeding US$1 billion (S$1.29 billion) at quarter's end; for many of these firms Nvidia remained among their top US stock positions.

The trimming came amid a sharp reckoning in the chip maker’s leadership: Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO on November 12 after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including with Nvidia employees and a woman suspected by the US Justice Department of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares had fallen more than 25% since The New York Times first reported in late October that Huang may have been targeted in a Chinese spy plot — even as his allies in Silicon Valley and President Donald Trump campaigned for his return to the top job, with third-quarter earnings scheduled for November 17.

The article notes that Nvidia’s shares were up 22% through end-September 2026, roughly double the gain of the US benchmark S&P 500 Index over the same period. Among other 13F filing highlights: Soros Fund Management sold about 206,000 Nvidia shares worth as much as US$47.4 million, with a remaining stake valued at nearly US$200 million; Jeffrey Skoll’s Capricorn Investment Group sold 9.8 million SpaceX shares worth almost US$1.5 billion; Alta Advisers added more than a third to its equity holdings (114 new positions); and WIT LLC — which manages part of the Walton family fortune — sold 2 million iShares ESG Aware MSCI EM ETF shares while buying 2.75 million Vanguard FTSE Developed Markets ETF shares.

The disclosures are drawn from 13F forms, which money managers overseeing more than US$100 million in US equities must file within 45 days of each quarter’s end — offering one of the few windows into how hedge funds and large family offices invest. George Soros himself has a net worth of US$9.7 billion per the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
items.title: Soros Joins Family Offices Selling Nvidia Last Quarter

items.summary:
NVIDIA has released two open-source projects—NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR)—as components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform. Both ship under Apache 2.0 and are in public preview, with conformance testing against Kubernetes 1.36. NVKE is a control plane for managed Kubernetes on GPU infrastructure; it exposes a REST API and controllers on a management cluster while customers manage clusters through kubectl or the nvkectl CLI. It uses upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm and Cluster API, is written in Go, and has no runtime dependency on NVKR. NVKR is a build system with declarative Definitions that produce executables, container images, Helm charts and node images for amd64 and arm64; its Recipes define validated combinations of software versions and GPU generations, and hosted workflows attach signatures, SBOMs and provenance to digest-pinned OCI references.

The NVKE architecture follows five stages: bootstrap (a temporary single-node kind cluster on a bootstrap host), management cluster provisioning via the NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo) requesting three servers, machine provisioning handled by NICo with CAPNICo as the Cluster API provider, release sets published and selected by name, and workload clusters each with their own control plane, etcd and node pools. Workload nodes must present an attested SPIFFE identity before receiving join credentials, per-cluster etcd encryption is available, and logs, metrics and traces are exported over OTLP via OpenTelemetry.

Adoption includes NVIDIA Cloud Partners Firmus and SK Telecom integrating both projects into AI factories; Mirantis, Rafay, Spectro Cloud, OpenNebula Systems and vCluster adding components to managed Kubernetes offerings; and Netris enabling NVKE for network automation. A local quickstart runs on one Linux host or VM (amd64 or arm64) needing at least 6 CPUs, 12 GiB free memory, 100 GiB free disk, Docker and virtual TPM support—no GPU or NVIDIA account required.

The article notes quality signals are certification rather than speed: no throughput or provisioning-time benchmarks are published. It flags worst-case concerns—the NVKE API serves plain HTTP on port 30080 with authentication off after install, plus the absence of a management-plane upgrade or backup procedure—concluding that these preview-grade security and lifecycle gaps make it not yet suitable for production.
items.title: NVIDIA Open-Sources NVKE and NVKR for Managed Kubernetes on GPU Infrastructure

items.summary: Francis Chu raises concern over the deaths of three cyclists on consecutive days (Nov 11 to 13), arguing that limited road-safety resources should be prioritised according to potential harm. He contends that greater attention and enforcement ought to focus on behaviours capable of causing serious injury or death, rather than placing disproportionate emphasis on the protective behaviour of those most at risk. Parliamentary questions and ministerial replies over the past decade have revealed two recurring areas of scrutiny: dangerous behaviour endangering others, and the habits or protective equipment of vulnerable road users. Chu notes that a pedestrian can be reminded to look carefully but this does not slow an approaching vehicle, while a cyclist's helmet offers little protection against the impact of a heavy vehicle. He asserts that safer road design works, pointing to evidence that Silver Zones have reduced accidents involving senior pedestrians by about 80%, and red-amber-green turn arrows have reduced accidents involving right turns by about 40%. Building on these successes, he recommends prioritising physical speed-calming measures at accident-prone pedestrian crossings, junctions and turning points; reviewing road layouts where vulnerable users interact with heavy vehicles; and giving greater enforcement attention to dangerous driving behaviours including speeding, failure to give way and unsafe turning movements. Chu acknowledges that road-safety education and personal responsibility remain important but cannot compensate for dangerous road design or inadequate control of vehicle speeds. He concludes that a road-safety system should not depend on everyone behaving perfectly, but rather be designed to minimise harm when people make mistakes.
items.title: Prioritising road safety for vulnerable users through design and enforcement

items.summary:
The Land Transport Authority (LTA) responds to a suggestion from K.T. Sandip, who called for replicating the innovative use of Marine Parade MRT corridor space elsewhere. LTA notes that MRT stations are an integral part of neighbourhoods and have been exploring how spaces in and around these stations can be used to provide amenities and opportunities for community activities.

The agency points to several initiatives already underway: through its Art in Transit and Spotlight in Transit programmes, commuters enjoy art, cultural performances, festive celebrations and community activities. Busking is permitted at designated spaces within MRT stations under the National Arts Council's Busking Scheme. Public transport operators have introduced various amenities including the Wellness Village at Tampines (DTL) MRT station, free-to-play indoor table tennis facilities at Esplanade, Marina Bay and Bayshore MRT stations, a dedicated dance space at Marina South Pier MRT station, benches along corridors, vending machines, and free health check-up equipment at Tanjong Pagar and Promenade MRT stations.

As part of the ongoing refresh of the Land Transport Master Plan, over 8,200 members of the public have since November 2025 shared their aspirations for the future of land transport. LTA welcomes further ideas on meaningful use of station spaces and will continue working with partners and communities while considering each neighbourhood's needs, available space as well as operational and safety requirements.
items.title: MRT stations more than transit points

John Urschel PhD ’21, a career development assistant professor in the MIT Department of Mathematics and former offensive lineman for the Baltimore Ravens before earning his doctorate at MIT, argues that building “math muscles” remains essential even as artificial intelligence becomes more capable. He recently used AI tools alongside human insight to solve two preprints on arXiv—one addressing the growth factor of random matrices and another examining worst-case behavior in Gaussian elimination—problems he says had stumped mathematicians for decades.

Urschel explains that his teaching goals center on helping students become strong quantitative thinkers, hone their problem-solving abilities, and assimilate big ideas within each discipline. He describes AI as a powerful collaborator with “unlimited resources” that can perform certain mathematics far more efficiently than humans, but he stresses the enduring value of independent understanding: when a machine produces a proof, its true worth comes from human comprehension, internalization, and communication of those ideas.

Drawing on his own education—raised by non-professor parents who did not know what a mathematician was until college—he credits technology like Google for giving him free access to papers by the world’s leading experts. Yet he warns that modern tools are “a bit of a double-edged sword,” because they can erode self-directed thinking and create false impressions of understanding, especially among tired high school or college students who might finish homework with “the push of a button” or write a 10-page essay without engaging the material.

Urschel frames AI’s development as overall good for education—leveling playing fields through accessible knowledge—but insists that productive struggle and human connection remain necessary. He identifies two reasons to keep studying math: learning how to think, which he believes will become even more valuable than mere expertise in an age of abundant resources, and community, since peer-based learning greatly enriches the experience.

As MIT prepares students for a rapidly changing world, Urschel says teaching cannot look like it did 10 years ago. He emphasizes that core skills—thinking, reasoning, and problem-solving—are needed “now more than ever,” underscoring his conviction that building these abilities remains important in the era of AI.
items.title: John Urschel on Why Math Training Still Matters in an AI-Driven World

items.summary:
Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, directing the supply chain and manufacturing that power its AI platforms across decades of partnership. She credits her team and a global network of manufacturers—including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor—for enabling NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. These relationships trace back years: TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998, while SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago.

For Shoquist, these ties deepen through challenges solved together on the factory floor as each generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it. She meets key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors. Recently she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award.

When asked how she describes her job, Shoquist says it is essentially a matchmaker: converting designs into the physical world by pairing precise blueprints with partners that fit their ramp style and possess the technology for very demanding specifications. A supplier must be financially strong enough to invest in NVIDIA's ramps, highly technical, and willing to do something never done before—three legs without which products cannot reach the needed volume and speed.

She illustrates this with Amphenol's cable cartridge, the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. It contains 1,500 small cable legs assembled to a quality level of less than 1 DPPM (defect part per million), produced on over a hundred automated lines at the speed and scale NVIDIA requires.

Explaining what changed as NVIDIA moved from selling chips to building systems and platforms, Shoquist notes that when it was primarily a chip manufacturer in an industry already at scale, selection meant picking the best technology match. As a data center systems company needing more partners—and entering new areas where supply base scale is still developing—she had to support and invest, as with Coherent and Lumentum, and create entirely new supply chains for products like co-packaged optics (CPO).

On the factory floor she has learned over 20 years that success depends on relationships not only with CEOs but also with production-floor people who understand manufacturing problems. Tight working ties let partners openly request better technical support, more quality engineers, improved designs, automation and material buffers—the result of two decades of learning from suppliers.

Demand for NVIDIA technology is massive and growing, so keeping volume up returns to relationships built on detailed knowledge of processes and people plus mutual trust. When pushing a line hard to increase volume, only then can NVIDIA ask for special favors surgically and credibly; success deepens the partnership.

Prioritizing resources means protecting critical components—wafers are essential as with air—and routing each chip from TSMC assembly every week based on factory performance. Every chip is tracked from its die identification number to the customer invoice, requiring suppliers to support that traceability process.

This discipline enabled NVIDIA to cut lead time from chip out at TSMC to system out at Foxconn and Wistron from five to two weeks when supply and demand require it. Shoquist likens the supply chain to a large circulatory system with pathways everywhere, empowering acceleration of any branch on demand.

She recounts one setback: preparing volume production for the compute board of NVIDIA GB200 with Foxconn and Wistron relied on an automated test handler—a completely new approach developed for high-volume throughput. During initial ramp, throughput fell significantly below plan, prompting Taiwan's operations director to disable the entire process and return to manual test loading while bringing in literally hundreds of operators to keep production moving.

The root cause spanned many elements: test tray assembly, design, automation hardware and control software, plus product yield—a difficult problem to resolve quickly. That is when NVIDIA executed its "swarm": teams from design engineering, operations industrial, product and test engineering, as well as Foxconn automation engineering, flooded the line with talent to redesign and reactivate it before the scale ramp hit.

Shoquist notes this is not unusual in operations; all NVIDIA teams are street fighters who know no organizational boundaries because "the mission is the boss." She finds operations exhilarating: an empowering place where her team constantly designs supply chain changes for strong new-product demand, always given needed resources, with only creativity standing between goals and success.
items.title: How NVIDIA's Supply Chain Builds World-Class AI Infrastructure

items.summary:
As President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors through new interim rules announced Monday that increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. The measures restrict not only the export of advanced chips but also Chinese firms' access to their computing power abroad—power they currently rent overseas to train artificial intelligence models. Under the new framework, these firms would need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers, allowing Washington to monitor whether such chips serve Chinese companies or are smuggled into China.

The rules pose a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on overseas compute in the wake of prior export restrictions. According to research by the Institute for Progress, at least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027. China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing would take necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.

The restrictions also strain South East Asian economies, where large numbers of data centres have recently sprung up. Singaporean firm Megaspeed—the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia—is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand; its former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The company denies the allegations, defends its business as "legitimate and lawful," and says it has retained external legal counsel for an internal investigation.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion, aiming to ensure sensitive technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis." Trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University warns that Malaysia and Thailand—whose data centre rollouts have been heavily driven by Chinese buyers—could be hit hardest, though he notes the rules are unlikely to derail the broader boom. Investment backed by major tech firms with clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient," says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft.

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but limited new construction, prompting investment to flow to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand; Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to capture spillover demand. These countries offer incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.

The restrictions arrive just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week. Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority, and its firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI—so much so that the Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months. Despite better compute access and financing from US companies, China still needs advanced US chips to keep its best AI models competitive.

The new restrictions have removed "one of the more practical routes" Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power, Bhattacharya said—though tighter controls could also push firms toward domestic semiconductors. This reflects a longstanding dilemma for Washington: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

The BBC contacted Singapore, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment. Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better and is exploring how to facilitate trusted access for local firms; Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls.
items.title: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China

items.summary:
Grindr, the world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app, launched its premium subscription service globally at a price of $120 (£91) per month. The company's CEO George Arison described it as "a very different Grindr experience" aimed at "a small community of users," and was unapologetic about the cost, stating: "I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not." This new tier follows existing offerings that include a free service plus two additional tiers costing between $22.99 and $44.99 per month.

The premium offering is part of Grindr's broader effort to become what it calls an "AI-first company," investing in artificial intelligence to build products more quickly and cheaply. The Edge service, which powers the premium tier, uses AI-powered features such as daily personalized profile recommendations designed to provide better matches and limit scrolling, plus insights into a user's compatibility with prospective matches and resurfaced summaries of past connections.

Grindr has been experimenting with Edge for much of the last year in markets including the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. On its earnings call earlier this month, the company reported that almost 400,000 users had registered for the service within the first 72 hours it was available for testing.

User reactions to the new pricing were mixed. In San Francisco, one user named Rybin said "The current premium Grindr tier is already really expensive," and described the newest offering as "really out of touch with the community." Another user, Adrian, added that the high cost "leaves a bad taste in my mouth." Conversely, a user named Michael stated: "The cost doesn't bother me," arguing that all apps have premium tiers and noting that high-end dating apps like The League can charge much more.

Arison defended introducing an ultra-premium tier despite concerns about dividing users into "haves" and "have-nots." He argued that Edge users being willing to pay more would allow the company to subsidize the product for everyone else, framing it as a personal choice. Arison also noted he has left open the possibility of increasing the cost in the future.

The AI strategy extends beyond Grindr's own products. In September, amid debate over AI safety across Silicon Valley, Arison said concerns about what he called an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic" prompted him to instruct some engineers to stop using Anthropic's technology. Although Anthropic is due to start selling shares to the public for the first time that week and its Claude Code tools remain in use at Grindr now, Arison said the company was on track to completely phase it out of his company's workflows by next year.
items.title: Grindr Defends $120 Monthly Premium Tier as It Launches Globally

items.summary: Actors across UK TV and film are to receive greater rights over their digital replicas under a new three-year agreement secured by Equity, the actors' union. The deal was reached with Producers Alliance for Cinema and Television (Pact) after years of talks following growing on-set backlash against AI use. Performers will now have the right to be paid when their digital replicas are used and to consent to whether such a replica is used at all. Approval must come from an actor before a digital double or alteration makes substantive changes to scenes involving agreed levels of nudity or simulated sexual activity, and producers may not use a digital replica during a strike in circumstances where consent is required. Contracts will now specify that permission applies only to a specific project rather than granting blanket consent over an actor's digital replica. The agreement also includes a 24% increase in pay rates for major films and a 9% increase for TV projects, alongside commitments to safe casting and audition spaces, training and reporting on sexual harassment, and adequate hair and makeup provision for artists of all ethnicities and cultures. Producers must limit access to digital replicas to those with a legitimate business need and use commercially reasonable efforts to protect them from unauthorised access, use or copying. The deal will be put to a vote among 8,000 Equity members, whose leadership recommends approval; it follows an indicative ballot last December in which 99% of members voted for industrial action over AI protections. Equity noted that digital replicas could instead be made from photography already captured during production without scanning artists. However, the union acknowledged areas a new agreement cannot cover, such as traditional digital scanning used later for effects, and said it did not establish explicit contract protections regarding using actors' performances to train AI systems.
items.title: UK Actors Gain Rights Over Digital Replicas in New AI Protection Deal

items.summary:
Japan has proposed a joint Asian task force focused on crude oil stockpiling, alongside a "Power Gulf Initiative" designed to deepen cooperation between Asian energy importers and their principal regional suppliers in the Middle East. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the effort as an equivalent of an Asian version of the International Energy Agency (IEA), announcing it at an Asia Zero Emission Community event that followed the ASEAN Summit, according to Reuters.

Despite the apparent irony of discussing crude oil stockpiling at a climate-focused gathering, Asian nations have acknowledged the need to safeguard their energy security by establishing an accessible oil inventory for use during supply disruptions. The initial agreement was declared last week at the ASEAN Summit, with members indicating that the scheme would include storage sites in Indonesia and Thailand from which ASEAN countries could draw crude when supplies tighten.

Withdrawals under this arrangement would operate on a ticket system: member states pay an advance fee to reserve the right to purchase specific volumes of oil or fuel from another member country's energy company-operated storage facilities. This model mirrors one already established in the European Union, which ASEAN cited as inspiration for its new initiative.

The stockpiling effort would be coordinated under Philippine leadership, according to Reuters reporting. Speaking on the matter, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. emphasized that sustainable and enduring energy security requires oil-consuming and oil-producing nations to act together—deepening information sharing and practical storage arrangements while committing to international law to keep sea lanes open and maintain fair, transparent markets.

The proposal reflects broader concerns stemming from the war in the Middle East, which dealt Asia its most severe blow due to heavy dependence on oil and gas imports from Persian Gulf countries. That vulnerability sharpened importers' focus on emergency stockpile security—a concern Japan has addressed for decades.
items.title: Japan Proposes an 'Asian IEA' to Protect Oil Supplies

items.summary:
This investigative report examines how large wildfire settlements may be undermining efforts to make forests less flammable through prescribed burning. It opens with the Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon Fire of 2022, which began as a controlled burn in New Mexico but escaped containment and grew into the state's largest wildfire on record, sweeping across more than 340,000 acres and destroying more than 900 structures. The resulting outrage has fueled litigation against the federal government, with Congress authorizing $5.5 billion in compensation for property losses.

The article traces prescribed burning as a critical tool to reduce catastrophic wildfire risk, noting that most burns are conducted safely—more than 99.9 percent do not escape their planned area—but warns that some will inevitably break containment. Studies have quantified the benefits: research from Stanford University found prescribed burns reduced wildfire severity by 16 percent during the severe 2020 fire season in the Western U.S., while a 2023 study showed low-intensity fires cut high-intensity wildfire risk by about 60 percent in California's forests. The U.S. Forest Service conducts roughly 4,500 prescribed burns annually across an average of 1.3 million acres.

The core concern is liability. Lawsuits against utility companies for billions have set precedents that now extend to other ignition sources, with courts often treating ignition alone as culpability regardless of weather or climate conditions. Liability standards fall into three categories—strict, simple and gross negligence—with Southeastern states like Georgia adopting the more forgiving gross negligence standard, while Western states such as Arizona, California, Nevada, Colorado, Idaho, Oregon and Washington operate under simpler negligence rules that create greater uncertainty for practitioners.

Prescribed fire advocates have worked to reduce liability through certified burn boss programs and funds. Over the past five years, California, Colorado, Oregon and Washington introduced training programs, with some states placing trained private burners under more protective standards. California and Oregon launched liability funds offering $2 million and $1 million respectively for damages from escaped burns when proper procedure was followed—though as of November 2026, no claims had been filed.

The report highlights a chilling effect on prescribed burning, particularly on state and private lands, which make up the vast majority of treated acreage at 84 percent. Protections for these land managers are narrower than federal safeguards, with indemnity rules varying by state and no protections existing for private contractors, tribes and nonprofits that must obtain their own liability insurance. The Nature Conservancy treats around 120,000 acres annually on its own land plus another 350,000 acres it assists government agencies with, but faces challenges maintaining coverage amid rising premiums.

The article notes a shift in Forest Service practices: the number of pile burns nearly doubled after Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon, though these account for only a tiny fraction of total treated acreage. Meanwhile, an analysis found no decline in prescribed burning overall despite growing litigation concerns among firefighters who worry about accountability and criminal charges.

The report concludes by contrasting Western states' progress with New Mexico's trajectory as a cautionary tale. Climate change further complicates the landscape, with a 2023 study from UCLA finding rising temperatures will cut suitable days for prescribed fire by 17 percent on average by 2060 in the Western U.S.
items.title: Wildfire Litigation and Prescribed Fire: The Liability Threat to Forest Management

items.summary:
A landmark 2014 settlement between the Bureau of Land Management, Bill Barrett Corp., and ten conservation and sportsmen's groups safeguarded about 90 percent of the Roan Plateau in Western Colorado from gas drilling. The agreement canceled all but two leases atop the plateau, refunded $47.6 million to the company, and closed roughly 34,000 acres—about 54 square miles—to new leasing through a revised Resource Management Plan written in 2016. This compromise ended years of protests and litigation that began when the BLM first proposed permits for oil and gas development on the plateau in 2007 and auctioned 55,186 acres in 2008 for more than $114 million, then the most revenue raised from a single lease sale in the contiguous United States. Now those protections face being unraveled under the Trump administration's push to open public lands for resource extraction.

The threat materializes through this December's BLM lease sale of four parcels atop the Roan, mandated by 2025's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law transformed federal leasing from a discretionary process into a mandatory one requiring quarterly sales in nine producing states and forcing nominated land to be offered within 18 months—down from six years under prior litigation. New leases would carry only stipulations baked into the outdated 2016 management plan, barring incorporation of newer science such as a 2017 study on energy development's impacts on ungulates or new surface-use protections requested by land managers.

The Roan Plateau rises 3,500 feet above the Colorado River Valley between De Beque and Rifle on Colorado's Western Slope, atop the southern margin of the Piceance Basin—one of the most heavily drilled natural gas fields in the West. Its public lands form an island of intact habitat surrounded by industrialized private land to the west; the protected eastern side hosts emerald-green alpine meadows, streams designated as Outstanding Waters including East Fork Parachute Creek where genetically pure Colorado River cutthroat trout spawn within parcels now proposed for leasing.

The rare cutthroat strain evolved to tolerate warmer water. Dean Riggs, who retired in 2020 after three decades with Colorado Parks and Wildlife, warns losing these fish would forfeit genetics needed as waters warm. Infrastructure development removes vegetation, increases stream temperatures, fragments habitat via culverts and roads, and can displace deer and elk for over 15 years even after wells close—pressures compounded by drought, wildfires, floods, and a state that just posted its lowest snowpack on record.

The BLM's proposed Oil and Gas Leasing rule would further compress public involvement from 90 days to a 10-day protest window, eliminate balancing of mineral development against wildlife habitat value, revive noncompetitive leasing, reduce bonding requirements, and require $1 per-page fees on protests exceeding 50 pages. The comment period closed Sept. 11, with the sale set for December 8th.

Opinions diverge: Chris Winter of Colorado's Getches-Wilkinson Center emphasizes the broad local consensus that was overridden by administrative action; Wade Haerle of Club 20 argues hunting, fishing, and oil and gas can coexist. Riggs expects drilling to proceed in previously protected parcels without breaking any deal, since permanent protection generally requires Congress—which has instead pushed to roll back protections—making the Roan an early warning of a strategy targeting less permanent land designations.
items.title: Colorado's Roan Plateau: A Landmark Conservation Deal Threatened by New Federal Lease Sales

items.summary:
At the RE+ event, Sunkean officially launched its ETL-certified 2000 VDC TRUNK-TTM system, extending its pre-assembled DC collection portfolio into higher-voltage applications. The company introduced this product to address challenges in utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) projects, where the DC collection network affects both construction efficiency and long-term connection reliability. Across large arrays, cable routing and repeated wiring operations demand careful coordination, which Sunkean addresses through two product groups: factory-assembled trunk systems and PV wire harnesses.

Designed for large ground-mounted solar plants, the TRUNK-TTM system integrates trunk cables and branch connections into a single assembly that collects DC power from PV strings and delivers it to a disconnect box. The design supports customized configurations to accommodate string positions, equipment locations, and project-specific layouts. Its vertical cable exits facilitate branch cable routing, helping installers follow the planned collection layout. By pre-assembling components in the factory, the system reduces the number of individual connection tasks performed on site, thereby standardizing connection work across the array.

The system’s current collection architecture addresses a separate concern: localized temperature rise. Where several branch currents converge directly at one point on the trunk conductor, this concentration can lead to excessive heating. TRUNK-TTM instead uses a staged approach, combining incoming branch currents before feeding the combined current into the trunk cable—a design intended to reduce the risk of such localized overheating.

Sunkean also offers copper-to-aluminum and all-aluminum options, giving customers greater flexibility in selecting conductors aligned with their project’s electrical design and material requirements. Alongside its trunk system, the company provides PV wire harnesses with multiple branch configurations—S-Y, S-X, and S-T designs—to accommodate different module layouts. Factory assembly of these harnesses helps reduce connection errors and maintain consistent installation quality, while matching the configuration to the module layout before construction aids contractors in preparing for installation.

For EPC contractors, the combined portfolio supports planning wiring assemblies around project layouts and better managing on-site workloads. For developers, it offers a way to balance construction costs with the need for reliable DC connections throughout the plant’s operating life. Sunkean frames these product innovations as reflecting its commitment to advancing solar connectivity, aiming to help customers build more reliable PV systems that support stable, long-term operation and greater sustainability.
items.title: Sunkean Unveils ETL-Certified 2000 VDC TRUNK-TTM System at RE+

items.summary: The 103 MW Huatacondo solar plant and its 98 MW/312 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Chile’s Tarapacá region have remained disconnected from the national grid nearly three months after an August cyberattack, per pv magazine. Chile’s National Electric Coordinator confirmed it activated disconnection protocols to protect the grid while an investigation continues. As of Nov. 14, both facilities had 0% availability and were listed as forced disconnections under request SDCF 2026100475, attributed to a cyberattack on Huatacondo; however, the BESS is still undergoing commissioning, so its unavailability does not count as an interruption of commercial operations. Lawmaker Cristián Araya Lerdo de Tejada submitted two formal requests for information—one to the Ministry of Public Security asking the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCI) about notification compliance under Chile’s Framework Cybersecurity Law, and one to the Ministry of Energy seeking technical confirmation of cyber origins, compromised systems such as SCADA and BESS management systems, unauthorized access, operational/economic impact, preventive measures at other facilities, and a timeline for reconnecting Huatacondo. As of Nov. 16, no responses had been recorded by the Chamber of Deputies, and no technical findings have been publicly released regarding the attack’s origin, affected systems, or resumption date.
items.title: Chilean Huatacondo Solar Plant Remains Offline After Cyberattack

items.summary:
Congress is nearing passage of a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill that would streamline the approval process for power plants and electric transmission lines across the United States. Negotiated by Democrats Sheldon Whitehouse and Republican Mike Lee, the measure has drawn support from both clean energy advocates—who see faster review for solar and wind projects—and conservative business and fossil fuel groups seeking to cut environmental red tape. It also bars presidents from cancelling offshore wind farms.

The bill has nonetheless fractured the climate movement and drawn its sharpest opposition from tribal nations. Critics argue it weakens the 1966 National Historic Preservation Act, a key tool tribes use to protect cultural, religious, and sacred sites outside reservation boundaries. Lawmakers such as House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries condemned the bill’s failure to safeguard tribal sovereignty, while Nevada Senator Catherine Cortez Masto said she would not ultimately vote for it.

The law requires federal review of projects that could affect historic properties within a broad radius—up to 5 miles from a project and hundreds of square miles in some cases. Supporters contend this process has become an excessive burden on infrastructure, especially transmission lines. Analysts Ben Schifman and Aiden Mackenzie of the Institute for Progress cite SunZia, an $11 billion wind-to-California line that took two decades to build and required a historic review covering twice the size of Delaware.

The initial bill version sought to avoid such delays by making tribal consultation optional, defining “traditional religious or cultural importance,” narrowing what counts as a visual impact, and limiting judges’ ability to halt construction. These changes drew immediate backlash from groups including the National Congress of American Indians. In response, negotiators amended the bill earlier in the month to make tribal consultation mandatory throughout review and to prevent the government from taking over reviews when tribes are slow to respond.

Opponents say these revisions fall short, with Ira Matt of the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers—himself a member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes—arguing that decades-fought protections remain eroded. Even so, some tribal nations see potential benefits: tribes with significant coal and oil reserves may welcome faster permitting for investment certainty, as did the Apsáalooke (Crow) tribe’s 2-million-acre reservation in Montana, while others hope to attract capital for renewable projects.

The article notes that even if the bill fails, the Trump administration is pursuing its own weakening of historic review through executive rulemaking. Analysts frame the reform as potentially the largest win for clean energy companies since the largely repealed 2022 Inflation Reduction Act—though one tribal advocate warned economic gains could never justify destruction of sacred sites.
items.title: Tribal Nations Push Back as Congress Fast-Tracks Energy Permitting Reform

items.summary:
Environmental advocacy groups have filed a petition urging the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to lower its drinking water nitrate standard from 10 milligrams per liter to 1 mg/liter, arguing that current levels pose a public health crisis across the country. The coalition—comprising organizations including the Natural Resources Defense Council, Union of Concerned Scientists, Prairie Rivers Network, and Food & Water Watch's Tyler Lobdell—cites research linking nitrate exposure over more than five decades to cancer, thyroid disease, fetal abnormalities, and blue baby syndrome in infants. One in three Americans, nearly 120 million people, are reportedly served water with dangerous nitrate levels, including those above the proposed 1 mg/L threshold—one-tenth of the current standard. A 2019 study estimated up to 12,594 new cancer cases annually attributable to nitrate in drinking water.

The petition's underlying science was analyzed by consulting firm One Water Econ, which produced a 43-page report estimating that adopting the stricter benchmark would cost $94.5 billion over 50 years for infrastructure upgrades and maintenance—though returns are projected at $364 billion in total benefits. The states with the largest impacted populations cluster in the West and Midwest, accounting for 62 percent of affected residents; agricultural powerhouses California, Texas, and Arizona lead this list, followed closely by Iowa, where approximately 42 percent of residents face nitrate levels above 1 mg/L.

The EPA responded that it would review the petition but noted its completed July 2024 evaluation determined the rule was not a candidate for revision at the time. The current 10 mg/L threshold dates to 1975 and was formally adopted in 1991, based largely on blue baby syndrome risk—a standard advocates argue fails to account for subsequent research linking nitrate exposure to other health problems. This reassessment effort has been politically turbulent: begun under the Obama administration in 2016, paused by Trump in 2019, restarted by Biden in 2023, and ultimately curtailed when a second Trump administration eliminated the responsible office.

The petition requests two immediate steps: an interim nitrate benchmark while the new limit is considered, plus enforcement of other federal protections like the Clean Water Act to rein in industrial agriculture. Climate change may worsen contamination as intense rainfall and flooding wash fertilizer and manure into waterways, while drought can concentrate pollutants; Des Moines-area residents already faced water restrictions for a second consecutive year amid high nitrate levels, and Illinois faces similar problems—where between 2021 and 2023 more than 2 million people were served drinking water testing above 1 mg/L. As Lobdell put it, 'People are paying with their health right now,' underscoring that the debate ultimately concerns where regulators draw the line between what is legal and what is safe.
items.title: Environmentalists Petition EPA to Lower Nitrate Drinking Water Standard Amid Cost-Benefit Debate

items.summary: On November 17, Nvidia announced that it has established a new board-level committee to oversee its national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management. The move comes days after the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang amid reports concerning his personal affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, which raised questions about potential national security risks and oversight of the AI chip designer's chip exports. Nvidia said that the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include directors Stephen Neal and John Dabiri. The committee is tasked with providing oversight for Nvidia's national security and global trade compliance programs and will work with independent legal, national security, and trade compliance experts.
items.title: Nvidia Board Forms Committee for National Security and Export Control Oversight

items.summary: The WTO's trade monitoring report for the period up to 30 June 2026 documents a sharp acceleration in both restrictive and facilitating trade policy activity. In 2025, members introduced 1,229 new measures; during the first half of 2026 alone, a further 1,048 were recorded, reflecting a substantially higher monthly pace that was broad-based across membership rather than concentrated in the largest economies. Trade-facilitating measures accelerated sharply: WTO members and observers introduced 466 such measures in H1 2026, exceeding the 391 recorded during all of 2025. These import- and export-facilitating actions covered an estimated USD 1.3 trillion (5.2 per cent) of world imports and reached a record USD 570 billion (2.3 per cent) of world exports, more than five times the level recorded in 2025 — much of this increase reflecting temporary measures adopted in response to trade disruptions associated with the Strait of Hormuz situation. Conversely, members introduced 333 new restrictive and other non-facilitating measures in H1 2026 alone, exceeding the 300 recorded during all of 2025; import-related restrictive measures covered USD 2.0 trillion (8.0 per cent) of world imports while export-related measures covered USD 794 billion (3.2 per cent) of world exports in H1 2026. As of 30 June 2026, the stockpile of import-related restrictive and non-facilitating measures introduced since 2009 and still in force covered USD 5.4 trillion of trade — equivalent to 21.3 per cent of world imports — while export-related measures reached USD 1.5 trillion (6.3 per cent of world exports). Both figures represent the highest levels recorded since WTO trade monitoring began, as noted by Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala. In most sectors examined, new import-facilitating measures covered a larger share of imports than restrictive and non-facilitating measures; exceptions were electric vehicles and photovoltaic cells, where major economies have been heavily competing for market share. WTO members continued extensive use of general economic support measures, with industrial and agricultural support remaining at historically high levels.
items.title: WTO Trade Monitoring: Restrictive Measures Surge While Facilitation Accelerates in First Half of 2026

items.summary: In response to rising scrutiny over social media content in India, Meta has strengthened its use of artificial intelligence to reduce offensive material appearing in users' recommended feeds on Instagram. According to a Bloomberg report cited by the outlet, Meta now deploys more capable AI models to review whether posts or videos should be surfaced to other users, with particular attention to violent and sexual-content recommendations as well as other sensitive material that violates its recommendation guidelines. The company reports that complaints about unwanted recommended content have nearly halved compared with a year earlier. To give users greater control over their experience, Instagram followers in India can now opt for fewer political posts or reduce exposure to sensitive content; Meta notes that adult-themed content was already excluded from recommendations by default in the country. These changes come amid intensifying government pressure on Meta following several content-moderation cases. The report highlights a growing tension between satisfying government concerns and defending free expression and fair moderation, including allegations led by youth activists of the Cockroach Janta Party movement that authorities are acting against social media posts related to student protests, while officials maintain such legal orders are necessary to curb misinformation and preserve public order. Separately, Indian regulators have asked Meta to remove child sexual-abuse material from Instagram and delayed a new WhatsApp feature over concerns it could increase online fraud risk.
items.title: Meta Tightens AI Content Moderation on Instagram in India to Cut Offensive and Sensitive Posts

items.summary: On November 17, 2026, Amazon announced plans to invest $7 billion in India's renewable energy sector by 2030. The company stated that this investment will make it one of India's leading corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy. As part of the initiative, Amazon revealed four new wind and solar projects across India, including its largest wind farm contracted in Asia to date. Overall, these efforts are expected to target over 2 GW of renewable capacity by the end of the decade.
items.title: Amazon to Invest $7 Billion in India's Renewable Energy Sector by 2030

items.summary:
In a podcast episode of Ideas in Development on Spotify, Apple Podcasts and YouTube, host David Lagakos discusses his new paper with Daniel Björkegren and Mitchell VanVuren. The team presents one of the first macroeconomic frameworks for thinking about AI's impact on growth in the developing world, showing how a country's AI future may be decided as much in high-income countries as at home.

The authors explain why developing countries risk being priced out of AI even as prices fall: because AI services trade on a global market, booming demand in rich countries can soak up supply and keep prices high relative to poor-country incomes. World Bank data on AI traffic suggests this may already be happening, with the poorest countries accounting for around one per cent of calls to frontier models while middle-income countries like Brazil are heavy users. Political pressure to slow data-centre construction would restrict supply, and poor countries would feel it through prices without having had any say.

A wrinkle that consistently changes the outlook in their model is satiation—the idea that we only need so much of some things. Macroeconomists rarely model it because centuries of growth suggest people seldom tire of anything. Using legal services as an example, if AI becomes very good at legal work, rich-country demand eventually plateaus, prices fall, and poor countries adopt more and catch up; yet Lagakos doubts this happens anytime soon. Satiation also has a darker side: if lawyers can only practice law while AI keeps improving with fixed demand, their wages fall towards zero.

Another striking result is that inequality often rises sharply within poor countries—the outcome the team worries about most. Where demand is fixed, substitutable workers lose, while the small group with complementary skills to AI—smaller still in poorer countries—does extremely well, echoing previous results showing ever-cheaper computers have driven up the skill premium.

Of the broad levers tested, only one consistently helped countries catch up: building skills that complement AI. Cash transfers raised living standards but growth paths were almost identical with and without them; a sovereign wealth fund financed by AI profits helps consumption more since payouts grow with profits but does little for productivity; subsidising AI moved the needle slightly while coming at an enormous cost and creating misallocation.

Lagakos's broader case is that macroeconomists are well placed to explore this terrain because the key interactions run through global markets, where what rich countries do absolutely impacts what poor countries do. Waiting for definitive evidence is not an option: by the time it arrives, policy decisions—and the damage or gains—will already have happened.
items.title: Who Will Get Left Behind in the AI Era?

items.summary: On Monday, a security researcher reported that some of the world's most visited websites—including those belonging to Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN (Cable News Network), Salesforce, and IKEA—were subverted in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones. According to researcher Scott Helme, malicious JavaScript was aimed at visitors to the websites of 178 organizations across various sectors through Optimizely, a website optimization platform. The scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency payment addresses with the attacker's wallet, skim card numbers as users entered credit card details, steal cookies and screenshots, and plant exploit code on iOS devices. Cybersecurity firm HudsonRock also said it had found evidence that the sites had served malicious code to their visitors. Salesforce said it was investigating unauthorized Optimizely script changes and had disabled them as a precaution; Equifax looked into the issue, stopped using Optimizely, and found no evidence its systems were compromised; IKEA sought to determine whether there was any potential impact on its digital services and customers. Reuters could not immediately ascertain whether the code was successfully used in each case or the extent of any resulting hacks. Optimizely, Apple, Zoom, HSBC, and CNN did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.
items.title: Popular Websites Subverted in Bid to Steal Crypto and Target iPhone Users

items.summary: On Monday, OpenAI announced an expansion of its Academic Researchers program, which will provide up to 200,000 researchers with free access to the company's frontier models. The ChatGPT maker plans to award 50,000 new grants on a first-come, first-served basis; each recipient may grant access to up to two collaborators. This expansion doubles the number of researchers initially offered when the pilot program launched in July. As part of its broader commitments to support scientific research, OpenAI points to ChatGPT Edu, which gives campuses access to the chatbot for academic purposes as more universities worldwide move away from blanket bans on AI use. The company also states that it will not collect data from users enrolled in the Academic Researchers program.
items.title: OpenAI Expands Academic Researchers Program to 200,000 Scientists

items.summary:
The owner of TG Jones is exploring a potential sale less than 18 months after completing its acquisition of the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith. Modella Capital, which also owns businesses including Hobbycraft, completed a deal to buy the 233-year-old business for £76m in June last year. The company pushed through a swingeing restructure to close more than 100 stores after receiving high court approval in July and has now moved to appoint advisers after receiving unsolicited expressions of interest.

Modella, which has closed about 150 of the 480 WH Smith stores since taking control, appointed Teneo Corporate Finance to review offers and undertake a market-testing exercise. An auction is planned for next year to avoid disruption through the key Christmas trading period. TG Jones employs about 3,500 staff.

Chief executive Alex Wilson said management and owner Modella Capital have jointly agreed to instruct Teneo Corporate Finance to review these offers, emphasizing their focus on providing a great customer experience during the critical Christmas period as they continue executing a turnaround plan improving performance month by month. WH Smith retained its almost 1,300 stores in train stations and airports, along with its website and right to its name.

The potential sale comes amid broader retail distress: Poundland's future remains uncertain after owner Gordon Brothers won high court approval for an extension of legal protection from creditors as it assesses three potential bids. Last month, Poundland's US owners filed a notice of intention to call in administrators while facing pressure to accept a bid that would save jobs and protect suppliers.
items.title: Modella Capital Puts Former WH Smith Chain TG Jones Up for Sale Amid Retail Distress

items.summary: In Columbus, Ohio, Ashley Baukman left a career as a licensed social worker to become an apprentice electrician through The Electrical Trades Center of Central Ohio. As one day out of every two weeks in class and the rest on construction sites under journeymen's supervision, she earns just over $25 an hour for time on the job plus a stipend for classroom days — already more than her social work pay, with prospects to nearly double it within three years. For Baukman, being the first college graduate in her family was once a source of pride; after earning only enough to support her blended family as a prevention specialist but not enough to pursue a master's degree required for school social work — while carrying an estimated $80,000 in student loans and five children at home — she found that the path simply wasn't viable. Her experience reflects broader themes among college graduates drawn to apprenticeships: Mike Hansen, 39, who left academia after seeing academics struggle with low pay for heavy teaching loads ($40,000 a year), now wishes he'd considered trades from his youth; and Michael Hughes, formerly of the Geek Squad, who found real breadth in hands-on work across diverse settings. Apprenticeships once aimed at non-college-bound students are increasingly seen as an attractive alternative to higher education: they require no prerequisites or prior experience, with acceptance generally based on contractor need. Demand for skilled tradespeople — especially electricians — is rising, fueled by a construction boom driven by data centers that has rapidly expanded The Electrical Trades Center's enrollment from 500 apprentices in 2022 to more than 800 today, prompting the shift from night school to daytime classes. Director Trent Parker notes several dozen currently enrolled apprentices hold four-year degrees and roughly 300 applicants have at least some college on their resumes; while he hasn't tracked the share of graduates over time, he's confident it's rising as sentiment toward the trades improves — a shift reflected in recruiting that once targeted students 'flunking out' versus today's focus on high performers. In 2023, Ohio's governor signed into law a requirement for licensed school counselors to visit training centers like this one, marking a significant step against the 'college or bust' mentality. The financial appeal is substantial: apprentices are guaranteed a minimum hourly wage starting at $23 with built-in raises topping out at $46 an hour as they reach milestones; journeyworker electricians earn well over $100,000 annually with overtime, and contractors sometimes offer incentives of $5 or $10 above the union-negotiated rate, double time for all overtime on some projects, and even rumored triple time. Union contracts provide retirement benefits and premium-free health insurance — a meaningful improvement over Baukman's previous benefit-less jobs. While data center work is expected at some point, reactions vary: Cekovich jokes about working exclusively there if the pay rumors hold true, while Hansen expresses concern over their heavy energy and water use and noise, though he expects ample work elsewhere in hospitals, schools, commercial buildings, and factories regardless.
items.title: Apprenticeships in the Skilled Trades: A New Path for College Graduates

items.summary: Tobacco group Imperial Brands is cutting up to 4,600 jobs as part of a major cost-saving drive tied to its increasing use of AI and other technologies. The Bristol-based company said this year alone would see 2,100 roles eliminated globally, with plans for a further reduction of between 2,100 and 2,500 jobs by the end of 2030. Imperial Brands has a global workforce of about 25,000 people; it will close its Langenhagen factory in Germany next year and has sold a plant in Taiwan, leading to 700 job losses. The company intends to outsource 400 jobs to Capgemini from its finance and procurement teams in Krakow, Poland and its global supply chain centre in Warsaw. Chief executive Lukas Paravicini described the cuts as part of a 'transformation' targeting at least £320m of annual savings by 2030, aiming to make the company more agile, data-led, consumer-facing and efficient through new software and AI. As cigarette volumes decline, the group—which is also behind John Player Special, Golden Virginia and Rizla brands—has been revamping its business toward newer products including vapes, heated tobacco and oral nicotine. The current cuts affect only a small number of jobs in the UK. Imperial Brands' total revenues fell 1.5% to £31.7bn in the year to 30 September, while profit before tax dropped 12.1% to £2.7bn; tobacco net revenues grew by 1.7% as prices rose 5.1%, offsetting a 3.4% drop in volumes. Paravicini noted that Blu vape product sales were growing at double-digit rates in the UK and expressed support for regulation, which he said would bring more market clarity. The article also references British American Tobacco's plans to cut about a fifth of its 47,000-strong workforce by 2026, including 5,500 job cuts plus outsourcing of a further 3,500 roles affecting a total of 9,000 employees.
items.title: Imperial Brands Cuts Up to 4,600 Jobs Amid AI-Driven Transformation

items.summary: According to a report by CNBC published on 17 November 2026, Nvidia has warned customers that proposed US legislation targeting Chinese companies' remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips could expose both buyers and the chipmaker to legal action. The company contacted chip buyers in recent months about the proposed Remote Access Security Act, citing potential legal risks arising from Chinese companies' use of computing capacity hosted overseas. Nvidia also told customers it would not sell chips to buyers renting more than 50% of their graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies. Separately, The Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia had verbally instructed data center customers to allocate at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese clients under future contracts. These reported warnings come as Washington moves to tighten controls on overseas access to advanced US computing technology. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced an interim final rule Monday aimed at preventing existing restrictions from being circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries. The agency said the measure, developed at the direction of the Treasury Department and National Security Council, would bring protections governing remote access more closely into line with controls on physical shipments of sensitive technology. According to the report, this regulatory action is separate from the proposed Remote Access Security Act, which passed the House of Representatives in January but has yet to clear the Senate. Existing US export restrictions limit shipments of advanced AI chips to China, while overseas cloud services can allow companies to access computing capacity without importing the hardware.
items.title: Nvidia Warns Buyers of Legal Risks Over Chinese Access to AI Chips: Report

items.summary: A wave of technology failures across the United States has fueled speculation about a coordinated cyberattack, prompting widespread concern. The disruptions began Friday afternoon when aviation authorities ordered the grounding of planes nationwide after an upgrade to the nation's antiquated air traffic control system overloaded its equipment, causing intermittent communications and radar gaps that led to a ground stop lasting more than four hours. Microsoft followed with an outage Saturday stemming from an issue during a network capacity upgrade, affecting many millions of people around the world before services were fully restored. United Airlines then announced a widespread tech problem on Monday afternoon (Nov 16) impacting departing flights, while several top US banks began reporting significant slowdowns after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects through the financial system; Chase stated its problems were not the result of a cyberattack and that it was working to bring services back online. The official explanations for these troubles emphasized no signs of malicious activity behind them, though public reaction varied widely as ordinary travelers grappled with cancellations and delays at airports including Newark Liberty International Airport, San Diego International Airport's Terminal 2, Chicago's O'Hare airport, and Charlotte Douglas International Airport. Personal accounts reflected both anxiety—Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, worried about the possibility that airspace or power grids could be shut down to cripple an economy—and resilience, with some travelers noting kindness among passengers and staff during long waits on the tarmac.
items.title: Tech and Aviation Disruptions Spark Cyberattack Fears Across the US

items.summary: Nvidia is set to report its first earnings since co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The third-quarter results will be the first since his departure and are expected after the closing bell on Tuesday, presented by CFO Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO. Investors will scrutinize whether customers continue to spend heavily on AI data centres amid concerns about sustaining the AI boom through the current crisis.
items.title: What to Watch in Nvidia's First Earnings Report Since Huang's Resignation

items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman praised Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang for his central role in advancing the artificial intelligence revolution, stating that it would be difficult to imagine the industry without him. Speaking at the 'Silicon Valley and the World' conference in Menlo Park, California, on 16 November, Altman expressed admiration for both Huang personally and the company's contributions to AI development. He described Jensen as long having been a hero of his own, while acknowledging that heroes have flaws but expressing gratitude for the company Huang has built. Altman emphasized how closely Nvidia and its chief executive are associated, pointing to Huang's ambition and the scale he has brought to the industry. When asked whether uncertainty surrounding Huang could produce ripple effects across the AI sector, Altman said he believed the industry would remain strong.
items.title: 'Hero of mine': Sam Altman praises Nvidia's Jensen Huang

items.summary:
The US Departments of Commerce and Justice confirmed on Monday that they were conducting a criminal investigation into Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed over suspected violations of semiconductor export controls. In a joint statement, the agencies said their Department of Justice and Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security would bring 'the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,' while also seeking to provide facts in response to inaccurate public reporting.

According to an official timeline, the Commerce Department launched its investigation in 2024 after detecting suspicious activity involving the diversion of chips and requested Nvidia sales records in May 2025. The following month, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on an internal 'no sell' list, while Bureau of Industry and Security agents conducted an on-site end-use inspection in Singapore alongside local law enforcement and interviewed then-executive Alice Huang. The Justice Department subsequently took the lead in the criminal investigation.

The statement also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick amid criticism from lawmakers and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over delays in placing Megaspeed on a formal export blacklist. Crediting Lutnick and Attorney General Todd Blanche, the departments said authorities under the Trump administration had charged 17 defendants in six cases involving 'billions of dollars worth of semiconductors' and increased monetary penalties for export-control violations 18-fold compared with the previous administration.

Earlier Monday, US President Donald Trump defended Lutnick's cautious approach ahead of his visit to Beijing, saying he had no plans to replace him while acknowledging differing views within his administration. 'One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blow up with China,' Trump said, adding that officials did not want to insult China just before arriving.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun criticized the move as 'overstretching the concept of national security and abusing export control measures.' He described it as 'a typical act of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction' that unreasonably suppresses the development of China's high-tech industries, harms Chinese companies, and destabilizes global industrial and supply chains, adding that Beijing would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

The investigation comes amid a leadership crisis at Nvidia following the resignation last week of longtime CEO Jensen Huang after reports linking him to an affair with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials suspect of spying for China.
items.title: US Confirms Criminal Probe Into Singapore's Megaspeed Over Nvidia Chip Exports

items.summary: As hyperscale AI data centers proliferate worldwide, governments face mounting pressure to balance accelerating computing infrastructure expansion against limited power capacity. In the United States and Europe, this tension has already produced policy responses: Denmark paused new grid connection approvals while New York State imposed a moratorium on permits for large new data centers. China instead treats the challenge as an opportunity, having included computing-electricity coordination in its 2026 Government Work Report for the first time and written it into the Outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030). The article frames AI expansion around an energy trilemma—uninterrupted power supply, maximum clean-energy utilization, and affordable electricity costs—which China argues is complicated by three structural mismatches. First a geographical imbalance: over 70% of its wind, solar and hydropower resources lie in the less-developed northern and western regions while roughly 60% of computing demand concentrates in eastern urban clusters. Second a temporal mismatch between fluctuating renewable generation and AI's need for stable round-the-clock operation. Third an institutional fragmentation between separately planned power and computing sectors.
items.title: How China Powers AI with Cheap, Reliable Green Electricity Amid an Energy Trilemma

items.summary: The article reports that China has been re-elected to the Council of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) for the 2027-2030 term. The results were announced on November 16 at the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference 2026, which took place in Dubai. In addition to its council seat, Chinese candidate Cheng Jianjun—a director of China Data Group Corporation—was also re-elected to the ITU's Radio Regulations Board. No financial or other numeric quantities are reported beyond these dates and terms.
items.title: China Re-elected to International Telecommunication Union Council for 2027-2030 Term

items.summary: On Monday, Chinese President Xi Jinping congratulated Zeljka Cvijanovic, Denis Becirovic and Darijana Filipovic on assuming office as members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH). The three were inaugurated in Sarajevo on November 16, 2026. Noting that BiH is an important partner of China in Southeast Europe, Xi said bilateral relations have maintained steady and healthy development over recent years, with political mutual trust growing increasingly strong and fruitful cooperation achieved across various fields. He emphasized his attachment to the development of China-BiH relations and expressed readiness to work with the new presidency members to deepen traditional friendship and mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries, steer bilateral ties to a higher level, and bring greater benefits to the peoples of both nations.
items.title: Xi Congratulates Members of Bosnia and Herzegovina's New Presidency on Taking Office

items.summary:
As COP31 entered its final week on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, President Murat Kurum — who also serves as Türkiye's minister of environment, urbanization and climate change — urged countries to deliver on existing climate-finance pledges. Speaking at a press conference on November 14, 2026, he said fulfilling current commitments is key to advancing climate action.

Kurum highlighted the climate finance decision taken in Baku under the 2024 UN deal: mobilizing $300 billion annually by 2035 and channeling those funds to developing nations. To help translate financing commitments into concrete action, Türkiye is rolling out the Climate Implementation Bridge mechanism in partnership with the UN Development Programme (UNDP).
