On China's role in the COP31 process, Kurum said Beijing has work underway on almost every topic within the conference's agenda and goals. He praised China as a leader in renewable energy — "very good" at it and leading the world on the issue — while also noting its technology know-how, willingness to share that knowledge with full transparency, rising renewable-energy investments, and falling costs in the sector.

As the two-week conference heads toward its conclusion on Friday, Kurum said Türkiye seeks outcomes across adaptation, mitigation and climate finance, expecting countries to track decisions taken, monitor results, and hold themselves accountable for the steps ahead.
items.title: COP31 chief urges climate finance action, highlights China's role

items.summary: Catherine Dobson, a former BBC Blue Peter badge presenter in Salford who met Michael Harvey while shopping at Asda in Rawtenstall, east Lancashire, in May 2012, is frightened and angry to learn that the police officer she calls her “master manipulator” will be released early after serving just a third of his sentence. Harvey worked as a detective in Lancashire police’s sexual offenders management unit; he first tracked Dobson through the police database—admittedly looking her up five times—and later messaged women on his work phone, telling one she was fit and that he would take her out for dinner while claiming they were victims of sexual abuse. He repeatedly lied to control her, including false claims about childhood abuse, post-traumatic stress from identifying body parts in Sri Lanka after the 2004 tsunami, and a rare cancer—all denied in court—alongside threats to kill himself if she ended the relationship. In February he pleaded guilty to coercive and controlling behaviour and misuse of the police database and was sentenced to 30 months; he was found not guilty of raping Dobson three times during her attempts to leave him. The judge said Harvey had caused significant psychological harm and that “the public need to see the courts punish police officers who betray public confidence and trust.” Both women were appalled by his early release under the government’s scheme, which they say he will complete by end of November; Dobson agreed when Andy Burnham changed the rules so that killers of officer Andrew Harper would not be eligible. She argues the exception should extend to serving police officers who commit such crimes and cited a Ministry of Justice investigation into comedian Russell Brand as evidence of inconsistent handling. The charity Women’s Aid said it believes as many as 5,000 women could be affected by early release of abusive partners.
items.title: 'Master manipulator' police officer should not be released early from UK prison, says ex-partner

items.summary: President Trump is currently attending the Asean summit in the Philippines before moving on to the Apec meeting in China, where he is scheduled to have talks with China's President Xi and Russia's President Putin. He has also indicated a desire to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The BBC's Jake Kwon assesses the likelihood of the leaders meeting for the first time since Trump returned to office.
items.title: Will President Trump Meet Kim Jong Un?

items.summary: Russia's Defense Ministry reported on Tuesday that its air defenses downed more than 1,400 Ukrainian drones during a second consecutive night of large-scale attacks. This figure represented an increase from Monday's count of 1,336 interceptions—the highest number Russia had claimed at any single point in the war—and reflected a broader escalation in aerial activity as both sides awaited a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks on ending the conflict that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022. Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces targeted the Kerch Bridge—a crucial span carrying military and civilian supplies between Russia and Crimea and also a symbol of Russia's annexation of the peninsula in 2014—for a second day running. While officials initially downplayed Monday's damage as insignificant, unconfirmed media reports indicated that Tuesday's repeat strike severely damaged one of the bridge's two arches; The Associated Press could not immediately verify whether any span had collapsed. In response to the disruption, Sergei Aksyonov, Russia's installed governor of Crimea, announced that traffic across the bridge has been halted and urged people to refrain from traveling toward it—though he made no mention of damage.
items.title: Russia Reports Downings of 1,400+ Ukrainian Drones as Kyiv Strikes Kerch Bridge in Crimea

items.summary: President Trump is traveling to Asia for a series of meetings covering trade and security matters. The trip includes a rare trilateral meeting with China and Russia, during which he will meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in a joint summit. Audio from the event was expected to be released later that day. The article contains no specific figures or dates beyond this framing.
items.title: Trump to Meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin for Joint Summit

items.summary:
Bilkis Bano, a Muslim woman who was gang-raped while pregnant during the 2002 Gujarat riots and saw her three-year-old daughter Saleha killed, has spoken of "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were granted bail. In a statement released Monday night, she said she had learned of the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back, noting that for 24 long years she had repeatedly stood up to fight for justice but now felt herself losing "the very justice I had fought so hard to win." She expressed fear of losing faith in the judiciary again and affirmed her resolve is for Saleha's memory and for women everywhere. The two freed men are Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, part of a group of 11 convicts serving life terms for the attack; both were released after being held more than 17 years, with one appellant described as having a severe handicap. Their release followed an order dated 28 October that suspended their sentences while they challenge a 2017 Bombay High Court ruling.

Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC her client was heartbroken and had no information about the case coming before the Supreme Court, warning each such event risks eroding faith in justice. The attack occurred on the morning of 3 March 2002 when Hindu mobs with swords and sticks assaulted Muslim neighbourhoods after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train at Godhra; Bano's village was attacked while she, pregnant with her second child, fled for safety. The riots continued three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims, including Bano's daughter Saleha, snatched from her lap and killed, plus a cousin who had given birth two days earlier along with the newborn.

Bano survived only after losing consciousness while attackers believed she was dead. The first arrests came in 2004 after the Supreme Court transferred the case to Mumbai, ruling Gujarat courts could not deliver justice. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, then Gujarat chief minister during the riots and criticised for failing to prevent the carnage, has consistently denied wrongdoing and never apologised; a 2013 Supreme Court panel found insufficient evidence to prosecute him, though critics continue to hold him responsible for the violence on his watch.
items.title: Pregnant rape survivor's heartbreak after two convicts granted bail in 2002 Gujarat case

items.summary: Twenty-five years after Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone premiered on November 16, 2001—when the then-11-year-old Emma Watson was chosen for Hermione Granger after about 10 auditions—the actress is marking the anniversary as far from the spotlight as possible. Born in Paris but raised in Oxford with no professional experience or interest in acting, Watson built a career that critics, audiences, and fashion industry alike embraced to avoid typecasting her. At 36, she has spent years away from acting after roles such as Little Women (2019), working with directors like Sofia Coppola, Darren Aronofsky, and Greta Gerwig, and starring in Disney's Beauty and the Beast. In an interview with Hollywood Authentic in September 2025, Watson described herself as perhaps the happiest and healthiest she has ever been while managing the aftermath of fame that arrived too early and intensely. She told the Financial Times that she felt caged and was frustrated by having to promote films whose creative processes she did not control, saying 'I didn't have a voice, I didn't have a say.' Watson also described the pain of leaving behind the close-knit community built around Harry Potter; after spending a decade working with colleagues bound by emotional ties, she found Hollywood's competitive environment deeply isolating. She acknowledged lacking the 'thick skin' needed to thrive there and felt as though her bones were being broken when she realized others focused on their own careers. During her time away from red carpets, Watson reclaimed parts of her life: in May 2014 she graduated with a degree in English Literature from Brown University, later resumed studies with a master's in creative writing at Oxford, and developed business projects such as Prada's Paradoxe fragrance (which she directed an ad for) and the premium gin Renais launched with her brother Alex. She is also a UN Goodwill Ambassador and maintains more than 70 million Instagram followers, showing sporadic commitment to the environment, the Palestinian cause, and trans rights—a stance that led to a public clash with J.K. Rowling, who called Watson 'ignorant.' Though Hermione's story returns this holiday season via HBO Max's new adaptation featuring Arabella Stanton as the young witch, Emma Watson remains in no rush to return.
items.title: Emma Watson Steps Back from Hollywood 25 Years After 'Harry Potter'

items.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) occupies a central position in the global competition for critical minerals essential to advanced technologies spanning medical equipment and military hardware, electric vehicles, and industrial batteries. As demand intensifies, the country has emerged as a focal point of geopolitical rivalry over mineral access. In this Special Issue, Mongabay journalists investigate how the contest for these resources is transforming governance, communities, and landscapes across one of the world’s most resource-rich regions. The series examines the intersection of deadly accidents at artisanal mines, international deals, conflict, foreign investment, and weak oversight as they converge to reshape the DRC.
items.title: DRC’s Critical Minerals Moment

items.summary:
Authorities in the city of Maebashi in Gunma Prefecture ordered school closures as officials searched for a bear believed to be its mother, after media reports said at least one person had been attacked. Officials captured a cub—one of two animals seen roaming residential areas—while the search for the adult continued. On X, Mayor Akira Ogawa urged residents to stay indoors and refrain from nonessential outings such as walks, warning of “an extremely dangerous situation,” especially in affected neighborhoods and surrounding areas. One person was injured; local media reported a man in his 50s suffered a non-life-threatening injury. The city’s schools were set to remain closed on Wednesday as a precaution.

Nationally, bear sightings have sharply decreased from the previous fiscal year, when a record 13 people were killed. In September alone, 1,759 bear sightings were reported nationwide, down from 4,766 cases recorded a year earlier. Experts attribute rising urban encounters to growing bear populations, declining rural human populations, and fluctuations in wilderness food availability that drive the animals into residential areas seeking food.
items.title: Bear on the loose in Maebashi prompts school closures and safety warnings

items.summary:
The article argues that South Africa's divide between its informal economy—where many people earn a living with weak or lopsided links to banks, supply chains and government systems—and the formal economy is a legacy of colonial and apartheid policies. This separation leaves small producers exposed when shocks hit, and while policy often assumes the answer is simply to formalise informal producers, the authors' research points to an alternative path: pairing organisations rooted in informal communities with those embedded in formal institutions.

The study examined what it takes for informally working smallholder farmers to reach the markets and institutions of the formal economy. Between April 2020 and March 2022, researchers followed eight intermediary organisations and 86 smallholder farmers across South Africa's Western Cape, Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Limpopo provinces through interviews and observation.

The research was led by an author who studies sustainability strategy, cross-sector collaboration and inclusive supply chains, alongside former students Mandy Rapson and Thanyani Ramarumo. Their study focused on social intermediaries—organisations that try to support small producers' access to markets but often struggle even in normal times.

The key finding was that farmers were well supported only when two kinds of intermediary worked together: a new national initiative able to raise money and deal with formal institutions, paired with long-standing local organisations the farmers already trusted. Neither could have succeeded alone. During the COVID-19 lockdowns, Limpopo smallholder farmers linked in this way kept or even grew their incomes, while similar unlinked farmers buried unsold crops.

The clearest test came in Limpopo, where 21 farmers were followed with different degrees of connection. Those linked to FoodFlow through Ga-Mphahlele Homecoming kept selling throughout the lockdown and some earned more than before; those without such ties were mostly left out—one farmer said simply they did not sell and buried all their produce.

The mechanism behind this success was trust. Apartheid deliberately separated 'white' and 'tribal' economies, and middlemen have often exploited that gap, so farmers had good reason to be wary of outside buyers. They would only deal with FoodFlow once a local organisation they trusted had vouched for it. When Umgibe's founder convened a meeting of farmers under a tree opening with a song, their trust in her was evident.

FoodFlow itself could do things no farmer organisation could: through its founders' networks it ran an online donation system within days and partnered with Oxfam and the Department of Social Development. By August 2020 it had raised more than R2 million (about US$120,000) and bought over 14,000 bags from more than 400 farmers in four provinces.

Yet FoodFlow lacked any relationship with the farmers it wanted to buy from. It needed partners—long-standing local organisations such as Abalimi in Cape Town, Umgibe in KwaZulu-Natal, Sigidi in the Eastern Cape and Ga-Mphahlele Homecoming in Limpopo—which knew which farmers had produce ready, how to collect it from scattered homesteads, and how to ensure payment arrived.

The authors call these two kinds of organisation 'bonding' intermediaries (drawing on close ties within a community) and 'linking' intermediaries (relying on looser ties to more distant institutions). The donations that funded the emergency supply chain have since gone, but once lockdown rules fell away in March 2022, so did the urgency. Still, everyone involved learned what a more inclusive supply chain could look like: farmer organisations gained contacts in distant markets and farmers saw what trusted local organisations can do.

The wider lesson concerns the informal economy itself. Much economic thinking assumes scaling requires formalisation—get small producers registered and contracted and markets will open—but South Africa's local informal institutions have carried farmers through decades of exclusion, holding up even in this crisis. The emergency supply chain worked by connecting them to formal institutions, not replacing them.

However, pairing only works with capable organisations on both sides of the divide; their sample also included three farmer cooperatives in Limpopo that had been set up mainly to access government grants and could not link members when the crisis came. A clear opportunity lies in public procurement: the government's school feeding scheme feeds millions of children daily yet mostly buys produce centrally, while attempts to procure locally—such as those in eThekwini—have often run into problems.

Organisations like the Southern Africa Food Lab and Seriti Institute have spent years connecting local farmer groups with the Social Employment Fund. The authors conclude that collaboration between intermediaries with complementary strengths offers a way to create more inclusive supply chains, noting that while a single organisation can sometimes straddle both worlds it is a lot to ask—so these experiments will be tested again by future droughts, floods or price shocks.
items.title: Informal and formal economies: lessons from COVID on how supply chains can connect the two worlds

items.summary:
L'élimination du paludisme est devenue un objectif réaliste pour de nombreux pays, et deux décennies d'améliorations dans la prévention, le diagnostic et le traitement ont réduit le nombre de décès liés à cette maladie transmise par les moustiques. Quatre avancées scientifiques majeures y contribuent : deux vaccins contre le paludisme, des technologies de diagnostic plus sensibles, la génomique des parasites et la surveillance de la résistance aux médicaments, ainsi que la surveillance environnementale et la modélisation prédictive à partir de données satellitaires. Ces progrès restent toutefois inégaux, en particulier en Afrique subsaharienne, qui représente encore environ 95 % des cas et des décès mondiaux liés au paludisme.

Les auteurs, chercheurs à l'Institut pour la lutte durable contre le paludisme de l'université de Pretoria, ont collaboré avec des programmes nationaux d'Afrique australe et constatent que les avancées scientifiques ne se traduisent pas toujours par des mesures efficaces. Trois obstacles majeurs sont identifiés : la prévision et la préparation (les alertes fiables ne conduisent pas toujours à des réponses opportunes), l'application des données scientifiques aux décisions politiques, et la sensibilisation face au changement de comportement, freiné par des obstacles pratiques et socio-économiques.

Depuis les années 1990, les chercheurs utilisent l'imagerie satellite pour étudier les conditions environnementales associées à la transmission du paludisme. En Éthiopie, en 2020, un système d'alerte précoce a aidé les autorités de Bahir Dar (nord-ouest de l'Éthiopie) à identifier une charge inhabituellement élevée et à se préparer.

Une étude menée auprès de plus de 7 500 personnes en Zambie et au Zimbabwe illustre le fossé entre savoir et action : parmi les participants adultes, 85 % ont correctement identifié les piqûres de moustiques comme mode de transmission du paludisme. Par ailleurs, 95,5 % ont pu identifier au moins un symptôme.

En avril 2025, l'Organisation mondiale de la santé a signalé que plus de 40 % des campagnes prévues de distribution de moustiquaires imprégnées d'insecticide, destinées à 425 millions de personnes, avaient été retardées ou risquaient d'être interrompues. Près de 30 % des campagnes de chimioprévention saisonnière du paludisme, qui devaient protéger 58 millions d'enfants, accusaient également du retard.

Trois fronts sont nécessaires pour combler le fossé entre la science et l'impact concret : renforcer les systèmes de santé, améliorer l'accès des communautés à la prévention et à une éducation sanitaire adaptée au contexte local, et assurer la coordination entre chercheurs, décideurs et programmes. L'article conclut que la prochaine avancée dans la lutte contre le paludisme ne dépendra pas uniquement des découvertes scientifiques, mais de leur traduction en décisions et actions ayant un impact sur la société.
items.title: Pourquoi les avancées scientifiques ne suffisent pas à vaincre le paludisme en Afrique

items.summary:
Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Greece and Austria announced on Monday the creation of a migrant deportation center in Rwanda where they will send foreigners whose asylum applications have been rejected and who cannot be returned to their countries of origin. The initiative is planned for implementation in 2027 as Brussels seeks to resolve one of its main migration stumbling blocks: the gap between removal orders issued by the 27 EU member states and those actually carried out.

The scale of this logjam is significant. In 2025, EU member states issued 491,950 return orders for non-EU nationals, but only managed to carry out 135,460 deportations — a success rate of just 28%, which Eurostat notes is the highest in the past 10 years. Reasons cited include the absence of readmission agreements, difficulties identifying people and obtaining travel documents, and lack of cooperation from some countries of origin that refuse to recognize nationality or readmit their citizens.

The Rwanda project introduces a substantial difference: it relocates to a third country people who have already entered EU territory, have no right to remain, and whose expulsions could not be executed. This follows the pattern of other European attempts to outsource migration policies, such as agreements with Libya, Tunisia, Morocco and Mauritania over the past decade.

The initiative builds on precedent but differs in model. The United Kingdom signed an agreement with Rwanda in 2022 to send asylum seekers there, but it never materialized after the Supreme Court declared it unlawful a year later due to risks of persecution or ill-treatment. Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen defended the new approach on Monday: "I believe this is a game changer" and argued that they would "regain control and remove the incentive for illegal migration." The legal framework now facilitates such expulsions since October 1, 2025, when the EU Council approved the new Returns Regulation, which allows establishing return centers in non-EU countries.

However, critics question both effectiveness and human rights. Estrella Galán of CEAR questioned whether European migration policy "should be measured by the number of expulsions," calling it "a true failure." She warned that these centers move people outside European territorial jurisdiction and away from protection mechanisms. UNHCR's Paula Barrachina agreed such centers cannot solve problems alone, insisting facilities must be temporary and no transfer occur if there is a risk of persecution.

Human Rights Watch's Judith Sunderland called it premature to speak of concrete guarantees, noting they do not know how the situation will be monitored. The agency reported that Rwandan authorities denied entry to an HRW researcher in 2024 — the fourth member refused access.

Rwanda's suitability is contested. Located in central Africa, Rwanda has undergone profound economic transformation since the 1994 genocide against the Tutsis and end of civil war. Its real GDP per capita increased by 245% since 2000 according to the World Bank, with economy growth of 9.4% in 2025 per Rwanda's National Institute of Statistics. However, on fundamental rights it has a long way to go: Amnesty International and others criticize its record.

The government of Paul Kagame, president since 2000 at the head of a Rwandan Patriotic Front-dominated government since 1994, faces criticism for repressing political opposition. Freedom House's report Freedom in the World 2026 gave Rwanda just 21 out of 100 points and classified it as "not free." The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights noted persistent prison overcrowding and limited access to health care, while Rwanda's National Commission for Human Rights reported detention centers at 134.3% capacity in its 2023-2024 annual report.

Reservations also arise within the EU itself. The European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA) warned in February 2025 that return centers cannot become detached from Europe's legal obligations, demanding individually appealable decisions and independent monitoring mechanisms. UNHCR considers them a complementary tool but recommends limiting transfers to cases where protection applications have been definitively rejected after fair procedure.

The article is published by EL PAÍS USA Edition.
items.title: EU's Rwanda Deportation Center: A Solution Beyond Its Borders?

items.summary: Ronald Drabkin's new biography aims to present the full life story of Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, who has long presented something of a puzzle. The central question it addresses is how this Harvard-educated admirer of the United States—who was reluctant to go to war—came to become the mastermind behind the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941. Drawing on recently discovered Japanese sources, Drabkin's work seeks to clarify this conundrum by arguing that much of Yamamoto's popular image simply isn't true. The book runs 256 pages and is published by Tuttle Publishing as a nonfiction title.
items.title: New biography of WWII admiral sets out to show his life story as a whole

items.summary: Plans for a new marine protected area (MPA) in Indonesia's Saleh Bay aim to turn nearly half of the bay into protection for whale sharks, which are classified as endangered by the IUCN. A recent population survey documented newborn whale sharks there for the first time, suggesting the sheltered bay may be a pupping ground—the first-ever such site recorded anywhere—and offering juveniles a predator-free haven rich in food to develop before adulthood. According to provincial government documents seen by Mongabay, the MPA would cover 90% of known whale shark hotspots in Saleh Bay, which lies near Mount Tambora on Sumbawa Island in West Nusa Tenggara province. The species has been monitored there since 2015 and typically grows to about 12 meters (39 feet), filtering roughly 6,000 liters (1,585 gallons) of seawater per hour while living up to 80 years and reaching sexual maturity only around age 30. The global whale shark population is estimated at 119,000–238,000 individuals; Indo-Pacific sharks make up 75% of the total but have declined by 63% over the last 75 years, while Atlantic numbers dropped by 30%. Experts cite targeted fishing, bycatch in nets and vessel strikes as key threats. KI's latest population assessment documents 174 individuals across 884 sightings, with fishers since August 2024 reporting five sightings of very small sharks between 1.2–1.5 meters long—only 33 such young have been reported in prior scientific papers. In May, the governor designated 73,165 hectares (180,795 acres) for conservation, extending an existing MPA to cover more than half of the bay's total 145,900 hectares (360,526 acres). The Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries is reviewing proposals ahead of what KI hopes will be formal recognition in 2027. Meizani Irmadhiany of Konservasi Indonesia emphasized that protecting this key juvenile habitat safeguards the species' future worldwide. Fishers have worked closely with KI on conservation and now benefit from growing ecotourism, training as guides; Hamzah, a fisher-guide from Labuan Jambu who caught a young shark in 2024, noted tourism has brought new livelihoods for those previously without work.
items.title: New Marine Protected Area to Boost Whale Shark Conservation in Indonesia's Saleh Bay

items.summary: Liam Slann and his father Brian Slann are standing trial over the alleged murder of 21-year-old William Holdback, following a drugs disagreement in April 2024. Both men pleaded not guilty to murder, though Liam Slann entered a separate guilty plea to manslaughter that the prosecution did not accept. On Tuesday, Liam Slann took the stand and told the jury he wanted to "get back" at Mr Holdback after the man swung a knife at him during an attempted drug deal in Welland, in Adelaide's inner north-west. He said his father drove him there against his wishes, that the alleged victim approached wearing a COVID mask, grabbed the bag of cocaine and stabbed toward him before the knife fell into the car. Slann described jumping out to chase Mr Holdback while trying to recover the drugs, saying he wanted to "hurt" the man but only to the extent of what happened, describing where the victim was stabbed as "very unlucky." He recalled stabbing the shoulder but said his memory became hazy afterward and that he had been in shock. Under cross-examination by prosecutor Nicola Moore, Slann addressed CCTV footage showing his father asking him where he had stabbed Mr Holdback, to which the son replied "everywhere," though he later denied saying this; Moore also put to him that he left the house with a knife in the early hours of the morning. The court previously heard that Mr Holdback was stabbed 10 times and was left crying out for help on the street. Trial lawyer Elizabeth Mansfield questioned Slann about his account, and the trial continues.
items.title: Liam Slann testifies in alleged murder trial of William Holdback

items.summary: South Korean shares fell more than 2% on Tuesday, with the benchmark KOSPI closing at 4,968.48 points — down 2.59%, or 132.02 points from its previous close — marking a nine-month low and a fourth consecutive session of losses. The selloff was driven by chipmakers dropping on US curbs against China and caution ahead of Nvidia's earnings, amid high uncertainty in the market. Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO earlier soured enthusiasm for AI stocks more broadly, dragging down US equities too. Samsung Electronics fell 3.3%, while peer SK Hynix lost 1.96%. Foreign investors were net sellers of shares worth 1.4 trillion won ($1.05 billion). Of the total 912 traded issues, 185 advanced and 709 declined. The won weakened to 1,338.2 per dollar on the onshore settlement platform, down 0.13% from its previous close at 1,336.5. In debt markets, December futures on three-year treasury bonds added 0.04 of a point to 103.52; the most liquid three-year Korean treasury bond yield fell by 1.2 basis points to 3.727%, while the benchmark 10-year yield fell by 0.8 basis points to 3.974%. Analyst Seo Sang-young of Mirae Asset Securities attributed the pressure to uncertainty ahead of Nvidia's earnings.
items.title: South Korean Shares Fall to Nine-Month Low on Nvidia Caution and US Chip Curbs Against China

items.summary: On Tuesday Amazon announced plans to invest $7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, significantly expanding its renewable energy portfolio as part of the country's transition toward a more sustainable and resilient energy future. This new commitment adds to an existing $4 billion already contracted in Indian renewable investments, making Amazon one of India's leading corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy. The announcement also included four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts: a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka; Amazon's largest wind project contracted in Asia to date; a 200 MW combined solar and wind project, also in Karnataka; a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh; and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan. Secured through Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), these projects are part of Amazon's existing $4 billion contracted portfolio in India, and once operational the combined capacity will exceed 2 gigawatts—enough to generate electricity equivalent to the annual needs of more than 3.5 million Indian households.
items.title: Amazon's $7 Billion Indian Renewable Energy Push and Its Carbon-Intensity Target

items.summary:
On November 17, 2026, NVIDIA, IBM and the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab) announced a joint initiative to develop a modular quantum computing codesign platform that combines quantum processors with accelerated computing systems. The collaboration brings together NVIDIA's accelerated computing technology and software with IBM's quantum computers—including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM describes as its most powerful quantum processor yet—while Fermilab contributes expertise in quantum error correction and high-energy and nuclear physics (HENP). DGX B200 systems are being installed alongside the IBM quantum hardware. The platform aims to let researchers develop and evaluate error-correction codes, decoding algorithms and quantum-classical applications, examine how classical computing can scale within modular architectures hosting multiple interconnected quantum processors, define requirements for future fault-tolerant quantum computers, and explore scientific problems in high-energy and nuclear physics.

Krysta Svore, NVIDIA's vice president of applied research for quantum computing, said that making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems linking quantum processors to accelerated computing. IBM's Jerry Chow noted that some fundamental scientific problems remain out of reach without quantum access, while Fermilab chief technology officer Anna Grassellino emphasized that accelerated computing and superintelligence will shape how algorithms are designed, errors studied and complex quantum systems coordinated.

Separately, NVIDIA announced a new decoding algorithm called TCBP-JOBS, available through its CUDA-Q QEC 0.9.0 library. The company said the algorithm can accelerate computationally intensive parts of quantum error-correction research by up to 13,000 times compared with existing leading algorithms, potentially reducing computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to just 45 minutes.
items.title: NVIDIA, IBM and Fermilab partner on modular quantum computing codesign platform; NVIDIA unveils TCBP-JOBS decoding algorithm with up to 13,000x speedup

items.summary: Amazon announced a proposed investment of $7 billion to significantly expand its renewable energy portfolio in India and strengthen its position as one of the country's largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy. As part of this, Amazon has also committed four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts (MW), including a 234 MW wind project in Karnataka — its largest wind project contracted in Asia so far; a 200 MW hybrid wind and solar project, also in Karnataka; a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh; and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan. Secured through power purchase agreements (PPAs), these projects will take Amazon's contracted renewable energy portfolio in India to more than 2 gigawatts (GW) once operational, equivalent to the annual electricity requirements of more than 3.5 million Indian households. The additional investment coincides with a new global target to reduce the carbon intensity of electricity powering its operations by 65% by 2030, against a 2019 baseline, part of Amazon's broader commitment under The Climate Pledge to achieve net-zero carbon emissions across its operations by 2040. Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi welcomed the investment as reflecting growing confidence among global companies in India's renewable energy sector. Currently, Amazon's Indian portfolio comprises 14 utility-scale wind and solar projects supplying carbon-free electricity to the grid, alongside 43 on-site solar installations across its facilities. Globally, Amazon has more than 700 wind and solar projects with a combined capacity exceeding 40 GW, making it one of the world's largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy.
items.title: Amazon's $7 Billion India Renewable Energy Investment

items.summary: Amazon announced plans to invest an additional $7 billion in renewable energy projects across India by 2030, expanding its wind and solar power portfolio. This new commitment builds on the company's existing $4 billion contracted investment in Indian renewables, which already comprises four new wind and solar projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts spread across Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. These include Amazon's largest wind energy project contracted in Asia so far — a 234 MW wind farm — alongside a 200 MW combined solar-wind facility, a 300 MW solar plant in Madhya Pradesh and another 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan. Once operational, the existing projects will have enough capacity to generate electricity for more than 3.5 million Indian households, with all four new sites backed by long-term power purchase agreements.
items.title: $7 billion Amazon India renewable energy investment and global carbon intensity target

items.summary:
Meta said it has recalibrated its recommendation systems on Instagram specifically for India, strengthening default protections against sexually suggestive material and content depicting violence. The company stated that these systems now use more capable AI models that check content before it is recommended, rather than waiting for users to report or hide unwanted posts. Meta described the work as having been ongoing over the past year and guided by what Indian users told them they want from their recommendations.

The changes come against a backdrop of scrutiny in India following reports that Instagram promoted child sexual abuse material (CSAM). In July, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) issued a notice to Meta ordering alleged CSAM advertisements—around 30 unique ones observed by a BBC Eye investigation—to be disabled, and even summoned Meta's global executives. MeitY also sent an advisory on October 10 urging that recommendation systems avoid showing only limited narratives and instead provide diverse information.

Meta said people in India now report recommended content about half as often as they did a year ago, though the company declined to share specific numbers or confirm when its India-specific changes went live. It also pointed to user controls such as Sensitive Content Control, which lets users opt for less sensitive material across Search, Reels, Explore, suggested accounts and in-Feed recommendations; Teen Accounts, launched last year, place teenagers in a 13+ content setting by default; plus options like the Hidden Words feature and blocking specific accounts. Meta noted that content breaking its Community Standards is removed globally, while unlawful content is restricted country-by-country.
items.title: Meta tunes Instagram systems in India to curb suggestive and violent content amid government scrutiny over CSAM promotion

items.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's push for the Delivery Protection Act (Intro 518) has prompted Amazon to threaten leaving its city warehouses. The bill would require covered warehouse operators in New York to hire workers directly for core delivery and warehouse services instead of outsourcing those jobs, with supporters arguing it would improve pay, working conditions, safety accountability, and establish a licensing framework for last-mile facilities. However, Amazon contractors argue the city itself relies heavily on independent contractors, challenging the legislation's premise. Kris Basmagy, whose company DashWave Delivery handles Amazon deliveries, analyzed City Comptroller records and identified approximately 85 contractors providing services including meal delivery and construction hauling to agencies such as the Department of Homeless Services, Department for the Aging, and Department of Transportation—compared with an estimated 40 contractors delivering Amazon packages across the five boroughs. Basmagy questioned whether subcontracting is 'so dangerous' if the city does exactly what it accuses Amazon of at a larger scale, calling the situation hypocritical. The report noted that this comparison does not demonstrate the services involve identical working conditions, contractual controls, or safety risks. Amazon contractors warned that leaving the city's more than 15 warehouses could threaten about 5,000 delivery jobs and 2,000 warehouse jobs. Mamdani urged the council to bring the measure to a vote at a Teamsters union rally last month, while Council Speaker Julie Menin expressed support for changes protecting workers while retaining jobs, stating she is 'determined to pass a bill that both protects these workers and keeps these jobs in our city.' The mayor's office did not respond to comment requests.
items.title: NYC Delivery Protection Bill Sparks Amazon Exit Threat Amid Contractor Dispute

items.summary: A bug that crippled Microsoft productivity software last week had been lurking undetected in the company's data centers since July, according to Charles Lamanna, the executive vice president who oversees workplace software. The malfunction began on Nov. 11 when Microsoft performed a routine rerouting of user traffic; just after 8 p.m. New York time that day, Teams videoconference and chat traffic was automatically redirected to the separate server system handling Outlook traffic. Combined with an unrelated loss of server capacity earlier in the week, this triggered the bug, which prompted servers to exhaust their memory after an unexpected surge in traffic (s3,s4,s5,s6,s8,s9,s10,s11). For 15 hours amid scattered server failures, Microsoft had little inkling it faced a larger problem, per a preliminary report issued late Sunday (s4). The company then spent another 15 hours identifying and beginning to roll out the fix — an eternity for a wired world reliant on its software (s5,s6,s7,s8,s9,s10,s11,s12,s13,s14,s15,s16,s17). Lamanna apologized early Monday in a post on X, offering more detail on what went wrong (s6,s7,s8,s9,s10,s11,s12,s13,s14,s15,s16,s17,s18,s20). At the nadir Thursday, more than 80% of the servers behind Outlook were unresponsive; such outages usually last only a few hours at most (s22,s23,s24). In this case it took longer because as soon as servers returned to service they were overwhelmed by waiting traffic and failed again (s16,s17,s25). By 11:30 a.m. on Nov. 12 — just as US business traffic was peaking — Microsoft realized the problem, then spent another 15 hours troubleshooting before deploying a fix (s4,s5,s16,s17,s18,s19,s20,s21). During the outage, work at many corporate and government clients ground to a halt: email inboxes failed to load, Teams invitations went missing, and workers resorted to phone calls and pen and paper (s3,s4,s5,s16,s17,s18,s19,s20,s21). The bug was worsened by automated systems that rerouted emails and user traffic to what Microsoft's system thought were healthy servers, causing the failure to appear there too; at 2:29 p.m. on Monday, Microsoft shares were down about 1% (s6,s7,s8,s9,s10,s11,s13). The problem was worsened by automated systems that rerouted emails and user traffic to what Microsoft's system thought were other healthy servers, causing the bug to show up there too; at 2:29 p.m. on Monday, Microsoft shares were down about 1% (s6,s7,s8,s9,s10,s11,s13). The outage was an embarrassment for Microsoft and a reminder of the risks of relying so heavily on a single technology vendor (s19). Lamanna said the bug wasn't caught because simulated traffic patterns and hardware in the company's labs didn't reflect real-world conditions; testing typically focuses on older, weaker systems to assess whether updates trip up the weakest link — but this bug is more destructive on newer hardware with more processing power (s27,s28,s29).
items.title: Undetected Bug Triggered Microsoft's Productivity Software Outage

items.summary:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained the reasoning behind the company's recent voluntary exit programme offered to more than 60,000 employees. Speaking on The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, he framed the initiative as a means of increasing individual agency during a period of upheaval, saying it was designed to let staff take control over their careers while Microsoft reconfigures itself around artificial intelligence. Announced last month and extended to eligible employees in the United States, Canada, India and the United Kingdom — roughly 27 percent of Microsoft's global workforce — the package drew questions about restructuring and shifting skill demands as AI transforms tech workplaces.

Nadella acknowledged that opportunity inside Microsoft is changing: while he said there would be plenty going forward, its shape may differ. He noted that team sizes and workflows will change, with Microsoft's roughly 200,000 employees needing to be configured in different ways as the company adapts. Drawing on his own journey from individual contributor to CEO, Nadella said he personally would not want to remain in a non-transforming team, viewing the voluntary offer as giving stuck employees a chance to make deliberate decisions rather than wait for circumstances to force one.

In an internal memo last month, Microsoft executive vice president Amy Coleman described the programme as providing eligible staff with 'a new choice' about their future outside the company while also giving organisations flexibility to adapt. The offer arrives amid a wider wave of AI-driven workforce adjustments across the tech sector; companies including Accenture, Amazon, Dell, Oracle and Microsoft itself have announced thousands of job cuts linked to artificial intelligence investments and shifting priorities since 2024.
items.title: 'Plenty Opportunities Going Forward': Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella Defends Voluntary Buyouts For 60,000 Staff As AI Reshapes Work

items.summary: Global technology giant Amazon has announced plans to invest an additional $7 billion (approximately ₹65,393 crore) in renewable energy projects across India by 2030, building on the $4 billion already contracted for such projects. The announcement covers four new wind and solar projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts: a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka—Amazon's largest contracted wind project in Asia; a 200 MW hybrid solar-wind facility also in Karnataka; a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh; and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan. These projects have been secured through power purchase agreements, and once operational they will push Amazon's renewable energy portfolio in India past 2 gigawatts—equivalent to the annual electricity needs of more than 3.5 million Indian households. The company currently operates 57 renewable energy projects across India, comprising 14 utility-scale installations and 43 on-site solar facilities. Beyond these new contracts, Amazon has globally contracted more than 700 wind and solar projects representing over 40 GW of capacity. On the emissions front, Amazon set a global target to cut the carbon intensity of electricity powering its operations by 65% by 2030 versus 2019 levels, as part of a broader commitment to net-zero carbon across all operations by 2040.
items.title: Amazon's ₹65,393 Crore Green Energy Investment in India

items.summary: A Financial Times report indicates that Nvidia's board is reportedly not considering bringing CEO Jensen Huang back as chief executive, despite calls for his reinstatement from US President Donald Trump and other Silicon Valley figures. The revelation emerged after the board launched an independent investigation into an alleged affair between Huang and Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials believe was recruited by China's intelligence agency; no action followed prior briefings about the matter. Although Huang had discussed a possible return with confidants—one ally reportedly assembling a 'war room' of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his reinstatement—his allies maintain that support is broad and that he has their backing, noting that "everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen." Trump endorsed the idea on Monday (November 16), stating Huang had "learned a big lesson" and would "certainly not mind" if he returned, while adding there was "a 'big group of people that would like him to return.'" Separately, a petition urging the board to restore Huang—or until compelling evidence showed his departure served Nvidia's interests—had gathered more than 188,000 signatures after his resignation. Signatories included Elon Musk and executives such as Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney; the site listed more than 9,400 current and 1,600 former Nvidia employees among signers, with more than 98,900 identifying themselves as shareholders. The petition's website noted that affiliations were self-reported and not independently verified.
items.title: Nvidia Board Not Planning Jensen Huang's Return Despite Trump and Musk Backing

items.summary: India condemned Turkey at the United Nations for what it called a "blatant and intentional" decision by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation's (OIC) Permanent Observer Mission to exclude New Delhi and other member states from consultations on drafts of a resolution concerning cooperation between the UN and the OIC. India's deputy permanent representative to the UN, Yojna Patel, said the exclusion was chosen deliberately rather than accidental, noting that even when some delegations registered objections in later rounds, facilitators still omitted select countries and basic procedures such as acknowledging inputs were "blatantly disregarded." While delivering India's explanation of vote, Patel called for an investigation into the working methods adopted by the resolution's facilitator. The draft resolution was introduced by Iraq with Turkey serving as its facilitator; it was ultimately adopted by the UN General Assembly with 112 votes in favour, six against and 39 abstentions. India voted against the measure alongside Armenia, Cyprus, Greece, Israel and the US. Patel argued that differences of position among member states are inherent to multilateral diplomacy and cannot justify such exclusion from consultations on matters before the General Assembly. In a thinly veiled reference to Pakistan, India also expressed regret that the OIC had "once again allowed itself to be systematically misused by one member state" to weaponise its resolutions against India through false allegations. Greece and Cyprus separately raised serious concerns about the conduct of negotiations under Turkiye's facilitation, with Greece's delegate noting that revised drafts were circulated without adequate consultation.
items.title: 'Blatant and intentional': India slams Turkey over exclusion from UNGA draft consultations

items.summary:
Bilkis Bano has announced she will challenge the Supreme Court's October 28 order suspending sentences and granting bail to two of the 11 men convicted of gang-raping her and murdering 14 members of her family during the 2002 Gujarat riots. Issued through senior advocate Shobha Gupta, a statement from Bilkis expressed shock and disbelief that the court passed its order without informing her or affording her an opportunity to be heard. She said she first learned of the development through press reports and questioned how the Supreme Court could issue such an order while ensuring her voice was not taken into account. This is the second time, according to Bilkis, that a case-related order has been passed without calling her or hearing from her; recalling this, she stated once again she cannot believe an order has been issued by the court without summoning her and listening to her. She added that she learned of it through press reports.

Recalling the events of 2002, Bilkis said she was just 19 years old when her world, her baby daughter, family, home and trust in humanity were brutally wrenched away from her. For the past 24 years, she said, she had fought repeatedly for justice — not only for herself but also for women everywhere. She credited discovering reserves of courage largely to the support and solidarity extended by a million voices, recalling walking from one courtroom to another while grateful each time she was vindicated and her faith in justice restored. Bilkis said she had gradually rebuilt her life with family and friends' love and support, yearned for peace and learnt to smile.

However, the latest order left her feeling that she was losing the very justice she had fought so hard to secure. She said familiar fears had resurfaced and she was scared once again for herself, her family and her children, while also expressing apprehension about losing faith in the justice system yet again. Determined, Bilkis declared "I will fight this order" — "I must," adding that her fight is for her children, who did not deserve to remain haunted by the fears and scars of the past for the rest of their lives. She invoked the memory of her daughter Saleha, killed during the 2002 violence, saying she deserved to live and that her memory demanded justice. Bilkis also said her fight is for women everywhere, asserting no woman, survivor or citizen should endure an eternal test of belonging and equality or spend a lifetime fighting for justice.
items.title: 'Order passed without hearing me': Bilkis Bano to challenge SC order granting bail to two convicts

items.summary: As India pursues its biodiversity goals under the 2030 '30 x 30' target adopted at COP15, researchers are proposing long-protected institutional campuses as Other Effective area-based Conservation Measure (OECM) sites to expand the country's protected-area network. A recent analysis indicates that India's protected areas currently cover roughly 28% of its geographical area through various regulatory frameworks—Wildlife Protection Act lands, Indian Forest Act forest lands, and Biological Diversity Act biodiversity heritage sites—which is close to but short of the 30% target; bridging the remaining gap requires shared spaces rather than conventional national parks and sanctuaries. OECMs fall under this category as a novel conservation instrument. The CSIR-NEERI campus in Nagpur serves as a case study, having been established in 1958 at roughly 46 hectares (about the size of 65 football fields), with dense vegetation that maintains temperatures about 3°C lower than surrounding areas and hosts more than half of India's bird species. Systematic sampling over a full year revealed 1,744 trees across 83 tree species, along with numerous microhabitats supporting insects, birds, and small mammals. Experts like Jagdish Krishnaswamy note that stable land tenure, established governance, restricted public access, and sustained management make such campuses strong candidates for OECM status, while India has already declared the Aravalli Biodiversity Park in Haryana as its first OECM site, with 13 more potential sites identified nationally. However, critics like Seshadri K.S. caution that OECMs lack statutory backing and face risks of becoming 'paper OECMs' or ecological sinks without committed management practices fostering coexistence among diverse fauna.
items.title: Institutional Campuses as OECMs: Expanding India's Conservation Network Amid Caution

items.summary: The global success of Nitesh Tiwari's film 'Ramayana: Part 1,' starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, has transformed a quiet hilltop in Kollam district into one of India's most sought-after travel destinations. The film's depiction of the mythical bird Jatayu fighting Ravana to protect Goddess Sita drew thousands of tourists to the Jatavu Earth's Center in Chadayamangalam—home to the world's largest bird sculpture. At its heart is Rajiv Anchal, a renowned Malayalam director and sculptor best known for the 1997 Mohanlal-starrer Guru, India's official Academy Awards entry. For nearly 10 years, Anchal trekked daily up the massive 1,000-foot-high rock to oversee construction of his vision: a colossal concrete sculpture measuring 200 feet in length, 150 feet in width, and 70 feet in height, built to symbolize women's safety and honour. Inside, he designed a multi-level audio-visual museum and immersive theatre. The film has turned Chadayamangalam into a bustling tourist hub; media reports put current daily visitors at around 3,200 to 4,000, with weekend numbers expected to exceed 5,000. Executives note a massive influx from North India, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka. Kerala Chief Minister VD Satheesan and the state tourism department recently invited film enthusiasts to visit, positioning it as prime for spiritual seekers and adventure tourists. The center operates daily from 10:00 AM to 5:30 PM (often extending to 6:00 PM on weekends), with full-day ascent packages ranging from ₹1,500 to ₹3,500; additional charges apply for rappelling, zip-lining, and paintball. Access is convenient: Thiruvananthapuram International Airport lies about 50 km away (with taxis and buses available), Kollam city railway station roughly 38 km from the site, Varkala railway station as a transit point, and Main Central Road (State Highway 1) for easy drives from Trivandrum and Kochi. The piece is by Livemint—News Desk.
items.title: Rajiv Anchal and the Jatayu Earth's Center amid Kerala's Ramayana tourism boom

items.summary:
The United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) on Tuesday designated Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City) as a Making Cities Resilient 2030 (MCR2030) Resilience Hub, making it the first urban centre in India and the latest in the Asia-Pacific region to receive this recognition. The designation enables GIFT City to share practical approaches to disaster preparedness, climate resilience and urban risk management with cities across India and internationally.

GIFT City spans approximately 4.05 square kilometres and is being expanded to more than 13 square kilometres, including its Special Economic Zone and Domestic Tariff Area zones. Currently, about 2,500 people live in the city while more than 28,000 work there. Sanjay Kaul, group chief executive officer and managing director of GIFT City, said resilience is fundamental to the credibility of a global financial centre, noting that businesses and communities need confidence that the city can anticipate risks, protect people and sustain critical services through disruption.

The recognition arrives as GIFT City seeks to integrate disaster preparedness into its urban development. The city joined the MCR2030 initiative in July 2022 with support from the Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management and guidance from UNDRR. It has completed the first two stages of the Resilience Roadmap and is now progressing through a third stage focused on implementation. A Detailed Disaster Resilience Scorecard assessment conducted in June 2023 informed the city's Resilience Action Plan, finalised in March 2024.

The preparedness framework includes disaster management plans at the city, building and utility levels, supported by a Crisis Management Group, an Incident Response System and designated officers. The city has conducted more than 15 mock drills to test emergency responses to earthquakes and fires, maintains a dedicated store with more than 36 types of emergency equipment, and operates an early-warning system integrating India Meteorological Department forecasts, alerts from the National Disaster Management Authority's SACHET platform, earthquake reports and inputs from a local weather station. Launched by UNDRR in October 2020, MCR2030 provides cities with technical assistance, partnerships and opportunities for knowledge exchange.
items.title: GIFT City Becomes India's First UN-Recognised Urban Resilience Hub

items.summary: The Supreme Court directed journalist Nikhil Wagle and Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut to file additional affidavits placing their explanations and apologies on record in a criminal contempt case arising from remarks they made targeting Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and the judiciary. A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi heard the matter, which was initiated on a petition filed by the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA). During proceedings, senior advocate Kirti Uppal, appearing for Raut, urged the court not to insist on his repeated physical presence, citing that he is a cancer patient undergoing chemotherapy and also has heart-related ailments. Senior advocate Indira Jaising, representing Wagle, sought consideration of her age and said she was unable to attend because of pollution; while speaking about journalism as a hugely honourable profession, the bench made a light-hearted observation before directing that any apology or explanation be formally placed on record through an additional affidavit. The contempt proceedings stem from remarks by Wagle and Raut concerning CJI Surya Kant after he declined to meet a delegation of Opposition leaders raising concerns over the Election Commission and protests in Delhi. Wagle allegedly posted an abusive remark about the CJI on X, subsequently deleted it and tendered an unconditional apology, while Raut alleged that judges attended political programmes organised by the ruling party and accepted hospitality from Chief Ministers. The SCBA approached Attorney General R Venkataramani seeking consent to initiate criminal contempt proceedings; he granted consent on October 15, observing that the remarks were prima facie scandalous and intended to lower the esteem of the Supreme Court, particularly the office of the CJI. On October 16, the court issued show-cause notices to Wagle and Raut, and at a hearing on October 28 permitted Wagle to appear virtually after his counsel reported that he had tendered an unconditional apology; Raut was directed to appear physically before the court on November 17.
items.title: Supreme Court directs Wagle and Raut to file additional apologies in contempt case

items.summary: The Supreme Court adjourned the matter concerning the relocation of the 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library (CSL) until Friday, directing that its books not be shifted in the meantime. Justice Sanjay Kumar expressed concern over how the collection was being handled, accusing the Centre of an ad hoc approach and urging respect for a heritage dating back to 1702, warning against treating two lakh books as if they could simply be discarded. The court's intervention followed suo motu cognisance of inadequate space allotted to the CSL under the Central Vista plan; it currently houses 8.5 lakh books but had been offered only two rooms in the Kartavya Bhawan-2 complex by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA). MoHUA directed ministries to vacate Shastri Bhawan, where the library is located, by end September ahead of demolition for redevelopment. The intervention was sought on 3 October after reports suggested relocation due to the proposed building demolition. Amicus curiae Senior Advocate Haripriya Padmanabhan urged a halt to the move and greater clarity from the Centre on space at the new location, requesting a breakup comparing current bookshelf usage with that of the proposed site. She also raised concerns about books kept at RK Puram in 'atrocious condition' for 15 years as part of the original collection. The court directed the Centre not to shift the books until its next hearing on 20 November, and required the affidavit filed by then be placed on record.
items.title: Supreme Court Halts Relocation of Central Secretariat Library Books Amid Heritage Concerns
